entry.title: What hour of the early morning
entry.content:
Moonlight gradually swallows the faint chill of early morning; on the marble-paved path newly lit by the breaking day, the dawn breeze pierces my exhausted body.
My body has swallowed the length of an entire night.

This is not a good piece of writing. Because what I am about to write is the present, not the past.

I don’t know how much of my literary flair remains after being eroded by time. Yet time has given me a new tone; I only hope I can still tell you the story clearly.

HJJ was my class monitor in high school.

She was very thin. We were in the same class in tenth grade, and fortunately, even after the classes were divided by tracks, we remained in the same class. Even though it seems I didn’t talk to her much in high school?—or perhaps it’s just that I didn’t talk to any of my high school classmates much—if I were to write about her, the first thing that comes to mind is still that I always ranked first in the class and she always ranked second, time and time again. I remember that except for one exam very close to the Gaokao, it seemed to be like this throughout the latter half of eleventh grade and all of twelfth grade.

Speaking of that exam, I was actually quite unhappy. I still remember walking out of the school gate and down that slope that afternoon, my heart full of resentment and complaints toward Teacher Huang. I remember thinking at the time, why did I do so poorly in math, and then I didn’t perform well in other subjects either, and so I got surpassed by her.

HJJ, of course, was overjoyed.

However, so many grades, such tiny differences in rankings, so many certificates of merit, so many people below the stage, so many gazes, so many honors—looking back through time, what is left? Only the joy of that moment, and the glory of bygone days.

I once thought solving problems was everything. To solve problems others couldn’t was to have everything. Until the morning self-study session on June 8th, the morning after the math exam, when for the first time I clearly understood what powerlessness meant. The math papers I had unfolded over the past hundred or so mornings had lost their meaning. I lay face down on the desk, filled with emptiness and sorrow. Only then did I clearly realize that I had poured too much emotion into something that was bound to end.

Another moment I still remember was right after learning about the class placements. I remember HJJ standing in front of me, happily telling me that we would be going to the same class again, though I can’t remember the exact words. As for the other few classmates who ended up in the same new class with us, I don’t seem to remember a single one of them—only her.

I feel like there has actually been more between HJJ and me after starting university. Through relevant admission policies, she also came to the same university as me.

I’m not sure if I factored in the possibility of being at the same school as her when I applied to this university. Of course, even if I did, it was a very negligible factor.

After all, I barely had a choice; not choosing physics as an exam subject meant I was left with nothing but trash majors, so other factors ended up being much more important to me.

We went to visit West Lake together. That was in 2023, not long after the semester started. The breeze brushed past the willow causeway, strands of green swaying; the lake water was in the distance, the mountains were further away, and the blue sky was even further still.

Strictly speaking, we went to the Zhejiang Provincial Museum on West Lake. What was inside? I can’t remember. I only remember being quite happy at the time.

And then it was '24. It should have been January of '24. I can no longer remember what kind of feelings I had for her back then. I still keep the photo I took with her at the time. She was dressed so beautifully. So beautifully. So beautifully. Beneath the night sky, she was even more beautiful. We had a meal together.

And what about me? What about me. I am just too terrible at doing these things.

I don’t know why. My emotions aren’t as rich as they were in high school. It’s probably an adverse side effect of emotional stability.

Sigh.

2025.7.1

On the first day of the second half of the year, as the sunlight hung low and fell from the canopy of the sky, memories suddenly surged into my barren heart, my restless heart, my uneasy heart.

I thought of the things that happened after the 2023 Gaokao. A pity only two years have passed; it’s not suitable to write about yet.

2025.7.3

Searching and seeking. Many, many contradictory thoughts are colliding and battling in my mind. It’s exhausting.

Can I really trust my own wisdom, and how should I attain happiness? Wisdom and happiness seem to be at odds.

I wish to pursue happiness, yet wisdom tells me that the way to attain happiness is not to pursue it. This would be the sinking of free will. It is really so hard for me to grasp the balance in between.

I wish to pursue happiness, yet I seem unable to use my own wisdom. This is the contradiction the book has given me.

相信自己的智慧，确信自己值得拥有幸福，这是自尊的本质。

To trust one’s mind and to know that one is worthy of happiness is the essence of self-esteem.

I feel myself sinking bit by bit, uncontrollably, into the abyss, and I don’t know what lies below.

The original word for “wisdom” here is mind, which in the English context seems to carry the meaning of “thought” to a certain extent. My stomach hurts so much. The original word for “essence” is essence. worthy of, on the other hand, has a relatively passive voice, carrying a lighter emotional coloring compared to “possess”.

The difference between wisdom and thought? I’m afraid there really is a huge difference. Although the author certainly tried their best to find suitable Chinese words, one really needs to read the original English text to understand the subtle deviations within.

I get it now! mind doesn’t just refer to wisdom! Because mind includes those irrational things! Fundamentally, this is deeply different from wisdom!

The more I read, the more I realize nothing is worthy of complete trust. How many schools of thought oppose one another.

2025.7.8

Back then, she also gave me a graduation gift. It was also the only graduation gift I received from a classmate. It was an elegant wooden music box shaped like a gramophone, playing a segment of Für Elise. Simple notes drifted before my desk, a red wooden box with a golden phonograph horn. I wonder what this meant? Für Elise can certainly be considered a universally beloved piece.

What happened during those few days of graduation? We went to pick up the guidebooks for filling out college applications; the wrinkled pages were covered in dense numbers and obscure names of majors I had never read before. The future was just as obscure and unclear, at least to me at the time.

Flipping through my photos, the graduation ceremony took place on June 12th. I have the complete audio recording of Principal Ju Zheming’s speech from that time, as well as a video of a dance performance, Love SOS, from the graduation ceremony.

And then, the only photos left are documents of the admission cutoff scores from eight days later. I want to cry so badly. Why was nothing left behind at all. Those few days. I want to cry so badly.

I found a photo from June 25th, of that gramophone. In a few days, I’m going to meet her again. I’ve been so nervous these past few days. I keep thinking about how I should polish my image. What I should say when we meet. What she will be like when we meet. Having not seen her for a year, how will she have changed?

Come to think of it, I’m actually more satisfied with my current hairstyle with bangs; for one, there’s just too much acne on my forehead, and covering it up really makes it unnoticeable at a glance, and for another, it really does provide better proportions.

Great, in the photos from June 27th, a video of this gramophone showed up. I really need to buy a music box as a return gift. Should I give it to her at the beginning or at the end?

The melody is much livelier than I imagined. Is she also much more beautiful than I imagine.

Speaking of which, she actually asked me to pick it out myself back then. Perhaps it’s less prone to mistakes that way, but perhaps it lacks a sense of surprise?

I still somewhat regret my mom meddling in my college application back then, though calling it “meddling” isn’t really accurate. Still, I really didn’t want any interference from her whatsoever. Because in this regard, she was definitely no wiser than me.

Laughable, truly laughable—back then, just to ensure I could transfer majors, I even wanted to waste dozens of points to apply for majors at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University. If you ask the current me, applying to this school, aside from satisfying a need for nostalgia and Zhejiang’s superior living environment, really isn’t good in any other way. But not having to leave my homeland behind is also very nice.

At the time, a very close online friend named Rikka strongly recommended that I apply to Hainan University; at least it’s a 211 university, and she was also at Hainan University. With my score, I was guaranteed to get in—majoring in Biotechnology. However, I’m afraid it was still the distance on the map that terrified me.

Here I attach The Road Not Taken

Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,
And sorry I could not travel both
And be one traveler, long I stood
And looked down one as far as I could
To where it bent in the undergrowth;

Then took the other, as just as fair,
And having perhaps the better claim,
Because it was grassy and wanted wear;
Though as for that the passing there
Had worn them really about the same,

And both that morning equally lay
In leaves no step had trodden black.
Oh, I kept the first for another day!
Yet knowing how way leads on to way,
I doubted if I should ever come back.

I shall be telling this with a sigh
Somewhere ages and ages hence:
Two roads diverged in a wood, and I—
I took the one less traveled by,
And that has made all the difference.

Speaking of which, I recently read MrNobody233’s blog and found that he wrote a lot about himself.

And I couldn’t be bothered to read it at all.

So I reckon nobody will actually waste their time reading the things I write either.

Then I might as well truly write whatever my heart desires.

Where was I?

Lately, I’ve been bitterly bogged down in all sorts of interpersonal relationships. And Coach Hou still hasn’t arranged a specific training camp schedule, so I don’t know how I should arrange my own itinerary either.

Looking at her photos, infinite beauty wells up in my heart. Infinite memories surge within me. I don’t know what she thinks. This is truly something difficult to describe in words, difficult to comprehend with rationality. Looking at her face in the photo, I can faintly match it to the silhouette in my memory. Although it’s a portrait photoshoot, she is so beautiful.

I think I finally understand what “I have never had this feeling before” means. This is truly a feeling no one else could ever bring.

She is truly a creation of God.

But what if she is no longer beautiful? What if, when we meet, she is far from what I imagined? Yet I really don’t worry at all. Just from talking over those few days, I am already certain of the beauty of her heart. It is a kind of beauty that grows day by day with the passage of time.

I’m really not sure what she thinks of me. But perhaps it can still be inferred: I’m still relatively confident. Optimistically, we’ll be able to meet on 7.12. Which is four days from now. God, that’s really so fast. The busy past month made me completely forget about these things, and now that I have free time, I suddenly realize that moment has drawn so close.

Looking back through our chat history, she has always been trying to talk me through things in various ways. I think I have indeed been talked through them. As for letting go: I obviously won’t ask her to do anything anymore. When we meet, perhaps I will simply express my deep and mellow feelings for her—this feeling is truly not something I could possibly abandon or change—without asking her to accept it. Nor will I rashly barge into her life to do anything for her.

Her existence is already enough.

I really don’t know what it will be like when we meet. I really don’t know if there will be a chance to meet on 7.12. As long as Hou doesn’t schedule training for us on the day of 7.12, I will definitely rush back, even if I have to rush back here the very same day, even if it’s really only for a few short hours at most. Wouldn’t that still be wonderful?

I’m not sure if I have changed enough.

However, I recently finally mustered the courage to seriously examine myself in the mirror. Acknowledgment and acceptance are the first steps toward change. I also finally picked up a toothbrush and toothpaste, which I hadn’t used in over a decade. A pity—I should find some time to go get my teeth cleaned.

She should already be back in Changshan by now. Imagining her location on the map. As long as she exists in the world, this world suddenly becomes so wonderful.

She makes the whole world wonderful.

For her, I will make myself a better person; I will change. For her—how wonderful she is, making my heart tremble.

It’s quite alright. Wouldn’t it also be good to meet once and have the rose-tinted filter shattered? But reading between the lines, I don’t think anything that shatters the filter too much will happen—those who believe themselves to be lacking are often not lacking at all.

When we meet, I must not look at my phone. I want to look properly into her eyes.

Let me put my emotions into words after all:

She said what I like is not her, but a more beautiful construct of memory that I built based on my memories.

Yet how is any emotion in this world not like this?

What a pity.

What a pity.

What a pity.

What a regret.

What a regret.

What a regret.

I still have to keep myself busy. It’s still caused by thinking that my current work isn’t important enough to me.

entry.title: 2024 ICPC Shenyang Travelogue
entry.content:
2024 ICPC Shenyang Travelogue

Summary: A humiliating, crushing defeat.

Day -1

On Thursday, I even purposely skipped my evening general education class, staying in the training team’s classroom from the afternoon all the way into the night, even though my mind was already a complete and utter mess by then.

I really, really, really, really, really, really, really, really, really, really wanted to win a medal. I really wanted to get a bronze medal. A shiny, golden bronze medal. But what’s the point?

That day, the airline canceled our return flight for the weekend night, so hyl and I rescheduled ours, while chy chose to come back on Monday due to an online exam or something over the weekend.

Then I found out that five books of templates and a printed copy of oi-wiki weighed slightly over 20 jin. That day I also asked my teammates whether they preferred 0-indexed or 1-indexed arrays, only to realize that which indexing to use really just depends on the specific problem.

Day 0

Set off for hgh on Friday morning and found that the check-in counters were different from what I saw in videos—they had all become self-service. Moreover, when returning from Shenyang later, I found out that arriving at the airport just half an hour early was enough, as security took no more than ten minutes.

That day I even stuffed a sweater into my bag, only to find it was completely useless. After landing, I realized a single down jacket was more than enough. It wasn’t cold at all.

At 7 PM that night, the three of us started a vp of last year’s Shenyang regional at the hotel. The bad news was discovering I had already done some of the exact same problems in individual practices… The good news was that we got bronze with 3+1 problems solved.

Then we got roasted by the upperclassmen in the group chat for still doing a vp when we were out on a trip. Looking back now, it was probably because we were under too much pressure at the time; if we had relaxed a bit, maybe we would have performed better instead. I have to say, the upperclassmen really had foresight.

Day 1

chy and I slept in until ten before getting up. Originally, we thought we’d have time in the morning to hang out or practice some problems, but the whole morning was just gone like that.

Check-in in the afternoon, then the warm-up contest.

Looking at the first problem of the warm-up, the problem statement was so lengthy that we definitely didn’t need to read it. Flipping forward, there was an interactive gimme problem where querying 100 times was enough. Though I did end up remembering 1923, a year that is perhaps very important to Northeastern University.

Then on the second problem, I misread the prompt like a total war criminal, thinking it was that computational geometry problem from 2023 Shenyang that nobody in the entire venue solved. Only later did I realize the original problem asked for the expected value, while this one asked for the expected value of the square, meaning x and y could be separated independently based on the properties of integrals. Didn’t even dare to think about it during the contest.

The third problem was from Zhihu, a 10100010^{1000}101000 dp, no clue. Only Team Jiangli solved it.

The fourth problem was a Nonogram. Our team was lucky enough to have brought two pencils (hahaha); I can’t even imagine how you’d do this thing without a pencil. Both hyl and chy finished filling it out in the last five minutes. Afterwards, hyl complained to me that he had practically memorized all the numbers by heart.

Anyway, we got bronze in the warm-up with two problems, the exact same warm-up bronze as last time in Hangzhou. And the exact same unmedaled “iron” in the main contest as last time.

Day 2

The seating was very cramped.

Sitting behind us was Zhejiang University’s Team “Next Life”. And we couldn’t overhear a single thing.

We finished the gimme problem in 8 minutes, 1 minute and 2 minutes faster than Team 2 and Team 6 respectively, yet it was of no fucking use. Team 2 took First Blood on Problem B.

After that, we looked at Problem B for quite a while. It seemed our construction wasn’t wrong, but rather our math was off, which led us to believe our construction was flawed. By the way, I saw other teams saying Problem B used a conclusion similar to CRT. What a shame—I had just talked to chy about CRT recently, yet neither of us realized it.

Problem E. After 3 hours, I coded an O(Tn2n)O(Tn2^{n})O(Tn2n) bitmask DP and submitted it. TLE’d. Didn’t think of the suffix min optimization, Gooooooooooooooooodddddddddddddd, we were just that close. I don’t know if the simulation chy wrote was correct, but it felt pretty sketchy to me. At the time, I only thought about recording the transitions from a specific state to the final state, instead of recording the transitions for all states in one go—with just a little special handling during elimination, it could have been optimized to answer queries in O(1)O(1)O(1).

Problem D. My two teammates quickly came up with the conclusion regarding inversions, but afterwards, they kept trying to figure out how to maintain the exact number of inversions, and even how to explicitly maintain the shift operations—which was probably downright impossible. It never crossed our minds that we only needed to consider the parity. Still too little experience and way too nervous.

Problem B. Constructed half of it in the very last minute, way past the point of no return.

In the late game, I was completely malding. chy kept arguing with me over the approach for Problem E, and everything was a mess. Also, when he was writing the dfs, I should have been watching over his shoulder, so that a few operations that could have been compressed into a couple of lines of XOR wouldn’t have been written out as dozens of lines by him. Mainly, I was just so frustrated, so frustrated, so frustrated, finding it so hard to accept the fact that we were going to get iron again. Ironically, in the last few minutes, when I knew we were truly doomed, I calmed down a bit and made a little progress on Problem B. For the first few hours, I was constantly overheating and under a mountain of pressure. I discussed my bitmask approach for Problem E with hyl, and we didn’t come to any real conclusion either. I also kept feeling that chy’s approach was too crude; we basically didn’t see eye to eye at all. If only T=1. T=10000 was such a massive bait. At one point, I even made the calculation error of 2^16=256. And the trash computer could freeze at any moment; just downloading a sample test case would lag out and spawn several windows. Next time, I need to try eating something during the contest to regulate my emotions. Though “next time” is very far away now.

The key issue was that I couldn’t disprove chy’s approach, relying only on a vague, gut feeling that something wasn’t quite right. During the contest, I never figured out how to optimize mine either; I was even thinking about how to optimize the exponent from 16 down to 9, rather than the 0 that the intended solution actually achieved. At the time, it did cross my mind that the intended solution was to move the entire dp process outside the queries, but I had no idea how to handle the queries under that setup. I simply never thought to process the states for all queries in one fell swoop instead of starting a separate state for each individual query, even though different states could clearly contain one another.

As long as we had solved a second problem before the three-hour mark, we would have gotten a medal. And we had a shot at all three of those problems, did half of each, and none of them were hard, none of them were hard, none of them were hard at all!

But what’s the point. Even if a bronze medal is useless, not even having a bronze medal—doesn’t that make me even more of a piece of trash?

Right after the contest ended, hyl and I rushed to catch our flight at the speed of light, only to find out we were an hour early.

Anyway, I left this heartbreaking city.

Conclusion

The revolution hath utterly failed; comrades must still endeavor.

Anyway, from now on I just need to do cf, as there are no more official contests left to play. Yesterday I did a div1+2 and only solved 2 problems. Probably because of too much stress—felt like my brain couldn’t even turn its gears.

entry.title: Magical Girl Lya Proposition Report
entry.content:
Problem-Setting Report for “Magical Girl Lya”

Originally, I wanted to imitate the format of the “Problem-Setting Report for <World’s Sleeping Fairytale>” from the ioi2024 National Training Team papers, but I realized this crappy problem has no depth at all and can’t imitate it in the slightest, so I’ll just write it like this.
This problem was partly inspired by P2572[SCOI2010]《序列操作》P2572 [SCOI2010] 《序列操作》P2572[SCOI2010]《序列操作》, and by the way, I temporarily made it harder on the afternoon before the contest.

Problem

Given a 01 sequence, with range flip and range assignment operations, query the longest 01 alternating substring within a given range. （1≤n,m≤5×105）（1 \le n, m \le 5 \times 10^5）（1≤n,m≤5×105）.

O(mlogn) Approach

Obviously, range flip and range assignment are standard segment tree template operations. The key to this problem lies in merging the nodes in the segment tree.

My way of writing it is to maintain, for the interval represented by a node, the lengths of the longest intervals starting from the left/right that begin with 0/1, and the lengths of the longest intervals overall that begin with 0/1. During pull (or pushup), taking the length of the interval starting from the far left that begins with 0 as an example: if its length equals the total length of the left child, we directly append the corresponding length of the interval starting from the far left of the right child that begins with 0/1 based on the parity of the left child’s length—whether it’s 0 or 1 follows the “odd changes, even stays the same” rule; otherwise, we just inherit it directly. The other three are the same. As for the length of the longest interval beginning with 0/1, we just need to take a max of the left and right children, and then take a max with the middle part. The middle part is formed by choosing the corresponding left value of the right child based on the right value of the left child so that they can be connected, and then we’re done.

It is indeed a bit of a heavy implementation, and I spent quite a long time writing and debugging it too.

Code

Old Version Problem

Given a 01 sequence, with range flip and range assignment operations, query whether the numbers within a given range are all 01 alternating. （1≤n,m≤5×105）（1 \le n, m \le 5 \times 10^5）（1≤n,m≤5×105）.

Old Version Problem O(mlogn) Approach

The range operations remain unchanged, but what we maintain only needs to be the node’s interval length and the lengths of the 0/1 strings starting from the left. Finally, we just need to check whether the string length equals the interval length.

Old Version Problem Code

Postscript

Originally, I was also thinking maybe there are some cheese approaches? For example, using bitset, which might achieve O(mn/w), so I specifically uploaded the first three new test cases with nm maxed out, and even raised the limit to 5e5, but up until now I haven’t implemented it, and no one else wrote it like that either. Though nine times out of ten it probably wouldn’t pass anyway, right? Even at the 2e5 level?

Honestly, I was super happy when zhw got AC during the contest. At least it proved that the very first problem I set myself for the very first contest I organized didn’t have any flaws. When he first got wa, I couldn’t help but start checking his code and my brute-force code during class, but thankfully he got AC in the end. By the way, the code he wrote was twice as fast as mine; I don’t know if it was because of fast I/O or something else, didn’t look closely.

Having said that, maybe it would be better to write the problem into the problem description?

And maybe adding a prefix to the test data points so they are tested in order would be good too?

As for this contest, I don’t know if it was because the problems were in random order, but the number of solves and the objective problem difficulty actually ended up being completely inverted.

Moreover, it was truly a pity that tiome and rainydyas passed the problem right at 22 seconds and 1 minute 35 seconds after the contest ended, respectively.

As for changing the problem title to “Bright Moon Shines O’er the Drifted Snow”, that was even a last-minute whim on the day of the contest (x. That works out nicely though, next time it will be “Fierce and Mournful Blows the Boreal Wind”, maybe next time I’ll have to write an announcement to remind everyone that the difficulties are in random order…

entry.title: Commemorating the 8th Anniversary
entry.content:
Deep grief forbids me slumber, bitter is this night so slow to wane.
The bright moon shines on drifted snow, the northern wind wails in its might and woe.
Fate moves on, sparing naught to stay; the passing years now haste my life away.

Though it is clearly just the turn of summer into autumn, the cold wind around me already bites like winter. I have no idea what the people on the sports ground are doing; all I can see are blobs of red and green squirming about, utterly meaningless. Retracing the old path, painful memories of the past along this road come surging back incessantly. It is clearly the past, yet while the past of back then was still mingled with a touch of nostalgia, the past of now leaves only pain. The pavement, the same gloomy hue as the sky, echoes the faint haze of the afternoon.

In the pitch-black night, upon the narrow, utterly empty stretch of snow lit starkly bright by the moonlight, it feels as though my despair lies buried. By a cold lamp, a lone soul in the night.

It has been eight years. To remember for a year or two might just be a child’s naivety; to remember for five or six years could only be called a lingering throe. But now it has been eight years, and I still cannot forget today. If in the even more distant future I still cannot forget, then what is this? Is it that I have never grown up, or is this truly that important?
I still remember today in '16, when the flower of happiness bloomed upon the barren, melancholic desert of my heart: zyx accepted my confession.
It has been eight years, and the day I memorized back then remains etched in my bones. It was a Sunday. First, I used the whisper function that qq still had at the time to ask if there was someone she liked. She confirmed, pressed for my identity, I was exposed, discovered, confirmed, and she must have replied with a smile that she had known my feelings all along—though even now, on the other side of time, I do not know if that was true or false. The joy that followed still glows faintly in my mind, which is now wrapped in gloomy gray. At least on that day, I was even skipping and jumping along.

Yon millet droops in rows, yon sorghum in the blade.
With lingering steps I go, my inmost heart is swayed.
Who knows me says my heart is full of woe; who knows me not asks what I seek below.
O distant azure Heaven, what man hath made it so?

Yon millet droops in rows, yon sorghum in the ear.
With lingering steps I go, my inmost heart as steeped in wine.
Who knows me says my heart is full of woe; who knows me not asks what I seek below.
O distant azure Heaven, what man hath made it so?

Yon millet droops in rows, yon sorghum in the grain.
With lingering steps I go, my inmost heart as choked with pain.
Who knows me says my heart is full of woe; who knows me not asks what I seek below.
O distant azure Heaven, what man hath made it so?

My inmost heart is swayed, swaying within my heart—God knows how much longer I am to remember this.

Afterward, this story quickly met an ending that should never have come so soon. This story died quickly—died in the tears that dried in the night, died amidst the vast distance and our aloof natures, died in a wide, sprawling marsh of regret.

Truly as clean as if it had never existed at all. Except for my memory now.

So I must keep commemorating it.

entry.title: Book Report on *The Case of the Speluncean Explorers*
entry.content:
Book Report on The Case of the Speluncean Explorers

The Case of the Speluncean Explorers is a classic work of jurisprudence consisting of a hypothetical legal case proposed by the renowned legal scholar Fuller along with the five jurisprudential opinions he wrote, as well as nine additional jurisprudential opinions subsequently proposed by Suber. Through reading this book, I have gained a preliminary understanding of the major schools of legal thought in the modern West.

First of all, what the different justices have in common is that they all take into account the public’s, as well as their own, varying degrees of empathy or sympathy for the survivors in the cave. Therefore, although the first Chief Justice, Truepenny, upon whom Fuller expends the least ink, and the legal textualism he represents emphasize the interpretation of the legal text itself and thus find the defendants guilty, he still thinks of relying on extra-legal executive power to grant them clemency from punishment. Even though “the provision of the statute is well known: ‘Whoever shall willfully take the life of another shall be punished by death’” (p. 18), sympathy and morality grant an exception, and the law takes morality into consideration. This school of legal thought strikes a balance between respect for the law itself and actual social realities—a balance that is more moral in nature than based on abstract reasoning. Perhaps the reason Fuller “appointed” him as the sole Chief Justice is also due to Fuller’s own endorsement of this view to a certain extent, just like the fundamental idea of his own doctrine: law and morality are inseparable, and there exists a middle way between traditional natural law and legal positivism. Truepenny seems to play a role that is both legal positivism, which considers only the law, and one that simultaneously considers morality. Even though requesting the intervention of executive power seems to violate the Western principle of the separation of powers, “it is in effect an instruction to the Chief Executive as to what he should do in this case” (p. 33). The other four justices penned by Fuller also explore the relationship between law and morality. Except for the third justice, who makes no decision, all the other justices distinctly represent the main viewpoints of a particular school of legal thought.

The second justice represents the main viewpoint of the natural law school. He first argues why natural law should be applied, and then argues the result of applying the spirit of natural law in this case. However, this approach of considering only the spirit of the law while ignoring the letter of the law does not seem to conform to the trend where, with historical and social development, the operability of abstract legal principles or spirits in specific affairs gradually decreases; after all, natural law itself can be traced back thousands of years to ancient Greece. The first part of his opinion is more akin to an argument for the basis of the basis of his own judgment. This is very similar to the subsequent justices, who all start from the periphery and gradually approach the core argument, though these procedures do not seem to be distinctly linked to the legal schools they represent. In his natural law viewpoint, law and morality are intertwined. In short, his final view is that, according to the legal spirit of natural law, self-defense is not a crime.

The fourth justice is the only one among Fuller’s five justices to render a guilty verdict—representing legal positivism, which tends to rely entirely on the law itself in judgments and severs the relationship between law and morality. This is completely contrary to China’s theory of the rule of law, as well as to natural law. Legal positivism emphasizes that moral considerations are irrelevant to the application of statutes, holding that the only question before the court is to confirm whether the defendants willfully took the life of another. At the same time, by pointing out that “not one statute in a hundred has any such single purpose, and that the objectives of nearly every statute are differently interpreted by the different classes of its proponents” (p. 36), the justice to a certain extent negates the singularity of legal spirit and legislative purpose pursued by natural law. However, purely pursuing the law itself and severing morality, much like the Legalist thought in ancient China, may not be suitable for the development of today’s society either. Meanwhile, emphasizing legislative supremacy seems likely to lead to excessive harm caused by evil laws.

The fifth justice “judges by common sense” (p. 40), yet relying purely on common sense makes the correctness of the judgment overly dependent on the correctness of common sense, which might lead to insufficient respect for the sanctity of the law. At the same time, if too much deference is given to the fact that among the public, “about ninety percent believe the defendants should be pardoned or released with a token punishment” (p. 43), this might result in too many factors influencing the law, making it difficult for justice to be served under certain circumstances, and in extreme cases, even leading to the tragedy of the Cultural Revolution. Nevertheless, as far as this case is concerned, casting aside cumbersome and obscure legal reasoning and relying on common sense does seem to achieve the wondrous effect of where hills and streams compound and no path seems to lie, dark willows and bright blooms reveal a village nigh. And in this justice’s opinion, law and morality likewise share a very close relationship.

In Suber’s sequel, there are two diametrically opposed viewpoints: Justice Tally’s utilitarian stance and Justice Trumpet’s stance that life is priceless. These two viewpoints can also introduce the famous thought experiment in ethics, the Trolley Problem. Justice Tally likens the actions of the cave survivors to “a profitable ‘bargain’” (p. 88), and uses a limit-based way of thinking to argue that preserving more people is often advantageous. Yet this is obviously difficult for human empathy to easily accept, because in Justice Tally’s argument, a person becomes a means to preserve the lives of companions rather than the life to be preserved—that is, the end itself. Just as Kant taught us, “Man cannot be a means; man can only be an end.” Undeniably, however, such pragmatism can indeed solve problems at times. Justice Trumpet’s view emphasizing the supreme value of life is similarly akin to the legal positivist view of the fourth justice, and both render the same guilty verdict. After all, what the law itself demands is the supremacy of the value of life.

Chief Justice Burnham, penned by Suber, emphasizes legal reasoning and the law itself—“we must discover what the law requires” (p. 55)—which is also similar to the legal positivist view of the fourth justice penned by Fuller. However, if one relies purely on abstract legal reasoning while completely disregarding the facts, one will inevitably arrive at absurd conclusions, such as “they could have eaten their own fingers, toes, earlobes, or drunk their own blood.” Perhaps this is also why U.S. Supreme Court Justice Holmes stated at the beginning of The Common Law: “The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience.”

Beyond debating whether the survivors are guilty, the justices also consistently debate whether the survivors’ actions constitute self-defense, excessive self-defense, or necessity. At the same time, they debate at considerable length whether the practice of casting lots to decide death is appropriate from the perspectives of procedural fairness, justice, and substance, which perhaps also reflects the Western judicial characteristic of valuing legal reasoning. Meanwhile, similar to Fuller, the final justice penned by Suber also withdraws from the judgment, though not out of indecision, but due to a conflict of interest. After all, if a conflict of interest exists, whether or not one makes a judgment contrary to one’s own interests, it is contrary to justice.

In summary, Fuller ingeniously uses this case of the speluncean explorers to showcase for us the main viewpoints of the several major mainstream Western schools of legal thought prior to the last century, allowing me to discern the grand design from the faintest clue; even if I am merely glimpsing a leopard through a bamboo tube, I have nonetheless benefited immensely.

entry.title: Zhexin of Zhijiang
entry.content:
Zhexin of Zhijiang — A Book Report on Zhijiang Xinyu

As a collection of short commentaries published in a column of the Zhejiang Daily by General Secretary Xi Jinping during his tenure as Secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee from 2003 to 2007, Zhijiang Xinyu vividly reflects the work deployments, ideological perspectives, and grand strategies of our Party’s General Secretary while governing Zhejiang; reading it brings immense benefit, leaving a lingering resonance that remains unforgettable for a long time. Looking back from the present day, one can even better appreciate the profound origins of General Secretary Xi Jinping’s determination and confidence—“In utter selflessness, I shall never fail the people”—as well as the evolutionary course of the General Secretary’s thought.

Over two hundred commentaries, every word a gem of wisdom; over one hundred thousand words of exposition, brilliantly diverse and splendid. Across a series of domains—ranging from economic development; the discovery, cultivation, and development of Party talent, the ideological style of leading cadres, the building of governance capacity, and the relationship with the grassroots masses; poverty alleviation; environmental protection, and the coordinated planning of ecological civilization construction and economic development; cultural protection, inheritance, exchange, and integration; the relationship between reform and development; the supervision of power, integrity, and corruption; the issues of agriculture, rural areas, and farmers, agricultural reform, rural revitalization, and the well-being of farmers; the practice of a series of basic principles and tenets of Marxist theory in leading cadres’ governance and the advancement of economic construction and development; the market economy; to a society under the rule of law—General Secretary Xi Jinping has made profound, clear, and distinctly instructive judgments of great practical significance, making the work well-worthy of the attention it has received from numerous leading cadres.

“From the masses, to the masses”—this is the subtle, unbroken thread running through the entire book. This central theme is most vividly reflected in the section concerning the “Three Rural Issues” (agriculture, rural areas, and farmers). “We must run our Party’s work line of doing everything for the masses and relying on the masses in everything throughout all aspects of the ‘Three Rural’ work.” (Page 100) On the basis of profoundly studying and understanding Comrade Hu Jintao’s Scientific Outlook on Development, General Secretary Xi Jinping pointed out the need to clarify that the core of the “Three Rural Issues” is the issue of farmers, which is an issue of enhancing farmers’ interests and safeguarding farmers’ rights. As an important cornerstone of our Party’s governance, farmers are of great significance to social stability. “Agriculture is an industry that pacifies the realm and steadies the hearts of the people, remaining ever the foundation of the national economy” (Page 191). Without industry, there is no stability; without agriculture, there is no wealth. It is precisely by adhering to “from the masses, to the masses” that Comrade Xi Jinping recognized that one of the major bottlenecks hindering agricultural development is the reality that comprehensive agricultural production capacity is relatively unable to meet the demands of our province’s scarce agricultural resources and the leveraging of comparative advantages (Page 109); the high-efficiency ecological agriculture pointed out by Comrade Xi Jinping as the direction for our province’s agricultural reform—distinct from both petroleum agriculture and natural ecological agriculture—is precisely a developmental guide formulated on the basis of fully investigating the actual resources of our province and adhering to a people-oriented approach. At the same time, with his unique strategic vision, Comrade Xi Jinping also recognized the crucial position of cities in resolving the Three Rural Issues. To this end, he pointed out: first, overall urban-rural planning to seek common development: “implementing the policy of industry nurturing agriculture in return, and cities supporting rural areas” (Page 103); second, nurturing rural areas to enrich villages, where such reciprocation is in itself also conducive to accelerating industrial development, rather than being a unilateral charity; third, gradually eliminating the difference between two types of people, namely citizens—that is, urban residents—and farmers; even if it is impossible for all farmers to live in cities, and even if the gap and difference between urban and rural areas cannot truly be eliminated, yet “though the distinction twixt town and country remains, the disparity betwixt them is minimized” (Page 189). In summary, in resolving the Three Rural Issues, Comrade Xi Jinping demonstrated his profound thoughts in just a few short commentaries, and even more so displayed his profound cultivation as an outstanding Marxist theorist.

“From the masses, to the masses.” Comrade Xi Jinping’s mass line is further reflected in the importance he attaches to the market economy and the private economy. He recognized the immense potential of abundant private capital for the development of Zhejiang Province, and the great significance of expanding the scale of private investment for enhancing the endogenous driving force of economic development: “We must further relax restrictions on investment fields; for some infrastructure construction projects with profitability, those that can be opened up should be opened up” (Page 14). “‘Zhejiang Merchant Culture’ is the soul of Zhejiang merchants” (Page 209); Comrade Xi Jinping recognized the increasingly prominent role played by the large number of Zhejiang merchants who emerged in the great tide of Zhejiang’s socialist market economy, along with the Zhejiang merchant culture born from their creative practices, in the development of Zhejiang’s enterprises and society. It is precisely by adhering to the mass viewpoint and basing himself on the perspective of the masses that Comrade Xi Jinping was able to recognize the vital force of “Zhejiang Merchant Culture” in developing Zhejiang’s advanced productive forces.

“From the masses, to the masses.” The mass viewpoint and the mass line are even more evident in Comrade Xi Jinping’s application of the basic principles of Marxism to the ideological and quality building of Party members and leading cadre comrades. Facing the temptation to abuse power, Comrade Xi Jinping pointed out that leading cadres must “establish the awareness that power is service, frequently ponder the important questions of where the power in their hands comes from and for whom it should be used, and consciously exercise power for the public good rather than for private gain” (Page 260). The sacredness of power has been widely respected since ancient times, and Comrade Xi Jinping’s exposition further emphasizes the intrinsic sacredness inherent in power itself. In the essay Being Good at Speaking with the Masses (Page 146), Comrade Xi Jinping conveys in a vivid and lively manner the need for leading cadres to strengthen communication with the people—coming from the masses and going to the masses—likening cadres who are divorced from the masses to suffering from aphasia. Behind language lie emotion, thought, knowledge, and cultivation; having an empty mind, putting on lofty airs, being severely divorced from the masses, and knowing only how to flatter in officialdom—these are things that leading cadres should spurn and utterly detest. Conversely, weighing another’s heart by one’s own, where hearts beat in mutual resonance—only when true sincerity is bestowed upon the masses shall the masses requite it with true sincerity. Only by winning the true sincerity of the masses can a series of the Party’s policies and guidelines be better implemented and carried out, can Party members and cadres carry greater weight in the hearts of the masses, and can the Party’s leadership be put into practice more subtly and effectively. In the essay Being a Confidant of the People (Page 139), from a delicate, profound, and meticulous perspective, Comrade Xi Jinping expounded upon the dialectical relationship between the macroeconomy and the hearth-lights of people’s livelihoods, arriving at the conclusion that “there are no trivial matters concerning the interests of the masses… we must shift our key concept of development onto the Scientific Outlook on Development, and onto putting people first.” To a certain extent, this clarified the problem of some Party members and cadres focusing solely on GDP while ignoring the actual livelihood of the people; it echoes from afar, to a certain degree, our country’s policies for the construction of spiritual civilization, social civilization, and ecological civilization, serving as a powerful guide for Communist Party members to serve the masses, educate the masses, and lead the masses. In addition, the viewpoints respectively mentioned by Comrade Xi Jinping in short commentaries such as Adhering to a Scientific View of Rights Protection, Handling Affairs for the People Aims at Serving the People, and The Voice of the Masses is the First Signal for Style Construction—namely, to “put people first and safeguard the fundamental interests of the masses; seek the needs of the people, seek the counsel of the people, and seek the sentiments of the people; take the needs of the masses as the primary requirement for style construction, and place livelihood issues at the forefront”—all possess extraordinary practical significance.

With his lively, vivid, figurative, and accessible writing style, Comrade Xi Jinping time and again expounded upon the numerous theoretical and practical requirements for governing Zhejiang Province; quoting extensively from a wide range of sources, he used aphorisms and golden sayings from ancient and modern times, both Chinese and foreign, to support his arguments, which undoubtedly enhanced the credibility and profundity of his own judgments. It deeply captures the essence of Chairman Mao’s literary style. Reading Xi Jinping’s Zhijiang Xinyu is truly of immense benefit.

entry.title: Audio-Reading Recommendations
entry.content:
When Fate Knocks at the Door

Just as Schopenhauer wrote in The World as Will and Representation, music possesses a magic that transcends time and space, and for thousands of years, countless souls have been intoxicated by it. There are myriad genres of music, and among those with the longest history is undoubtedly the magnificent symphony; and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5, or as it is more popularly known, the Fate Symphony, is one of the most resplendent jewels in the crown of music.

This is perhaps the most household melody in the world: three low notes, trailed by an even deeper tone. No one could fail to feel a tremor in their heart, sensing that the God of Fate might have already knocked upon the door, bearing a scythe and wearing a faint smile. The grandeur and vigor of the violins playing in concert are unmatched by any other piece; ten thousand sounds erupt at once, yet here alone, it never feels cacophonous. Countless times, late at night, I have listened to this melody that has been played countless times over the centuries—that soaring height and that deep low shining upon each other, that fervent heat and that airy lightness harmonizing with one another, that hope reignited and that ceaseless struggle, like a transverse flute drifting over post-war ruins, and that melodious tune after a beautiful, dreamlike victory… Never once has our will been defeated; instead, it merely repeats the struggle again and again, and yet again… Even amidst an earth-shattering unison, the will to fight is never ultimately destroyed.

The first movement is undoubtedly the most universally acclaimed, yet the works of classical composers are often not confined to just a few minutes. With the pen in his hand, Beethoven used ink upon mere inches of sheet music to paint a colossal ship of victory sailing toward the heavens. Repeating time and time again, its immensely imaginative beauty, unbound by lyrics, sincerely grants me healing. And beneath the main, soaring tones, the looping, recurring melodies or the striking of the timpani are nothing short of perfection.

Perhaps it is precisely because nothing is spoken that so much is said; and once spoken, it can no longer be expressed—this is probably the charm of pure music. Therefore, with great solemnity and enthusiasm, I recommend Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5.

My own shallow insights will surely be laughable to the experts

entry.title: Autobiography
entry.content:
Personal Autobiography

Born in Changshan, the westernmost small county by longitude in Zhejiang’s territory, with a population merely 2.1% that of Hangzhou, the childhood life in my memory was filled with verdant hills, clear waters, and babbling brooks; that joyful laughter, that free breeze filling the fields after school, have traversed more than ten years of time, surging in my heart, never having left.

Yet before starting primary school, I lived with my mom and dad, in Hangzhou, in Lishui, at one express delivery station after another; my father’s broad, towering shoulders and my mother’s smiling face constructed an unbreakable line of defense against setbacks in my childhood, escorting my, jewel-like, precious childhood along the bustling journeys. On the night before summer vacation began, which for me at the time was already deep into the night, I sat on the bed, covered by the quilt, reading Souvenirs Entomologiques, thinking of my father approaching me in a speeding minivan. Waiting, waiting, waiting, the sound of a horn tore through the silence of the night sky, coming from the doorway, startling my grandparents and a flock of birds suitable as poetic imagery. What was I thinking? I hoped Mom and Dad would read to me by my bedside, however, they took me away that very night.

Examining it many years later, this seemingly simple little matter practically contains the code that runs through my life and character. First: I was reading. I was reading popular science books like Souvenirs Entomologiques, STEM-related works; it turns out God had long since planted the seeds of exploring the world in my heart, which also echoed from afar my subsequent love for sci-fi, and grafted onto my curiosity and exploration of the computer world. Second: one of my implicit purposes was to make Mom and Dad think that I was a studious, good child. The vines of caring about others’ gazes, which still entangle me to this day, had also long sprouted in my young heart. My preoccupation with the gaze of others, for one, ought to lie in the drastic change of environment after leaving my parents in the first grade—this being the external cause; and second, the drastic change in personality with the onset of puberty—this being the internal cause. Listening to what my mother and my residual memories tell me, the even younger me was extroverted, second to none.

Has the past me of the past truly disappeared? Not necessarily. In the eyes of my past self, in the clothing shop named “Yi Zhi Du Xiu”, that inquiry to the boss—for an elementary school extracurricular practical research course based on the punning use of Chinese characters, made ahead of that close companion of mine—was the inner me, the me of the distant past, successfully taking control of my throat, and making a sound. Just as he can now only scream silently in my heart.

Silent screams will eventually break through a cage made of iron. In the sixth grade, those three words I “screamed” at the teacher, “I forgot!”, left a vivid impression. Her subsequent, head-on, endless berating of me, or whatever other word you want to use, her figure standing on the podium, her eyes harboring disgust. God, it still makes the present me want to slap her across the face. Did she not understand my kindness? Did she not understand the cause and effect? Did she not know what consequences berating an elementary school student without sufficient reason would bring? Even if you apologize later, how can you completely restore the wound? This was my desperate leap of a cornered dog, of a sixth-grade elementary school student, and the loss of control of a teacher who possessed authority and power in front of students.

I have reason to deduce that, from then until now, I am “afraid of all teachers.”

The fear of relatively unfamiliar elders seems to have a reluctant answer, so where does the avoidance of peers begin? At least in elementary school, I possessed an absolutely normal social life.

Boarding is a challenge for any new middle schooler, and for me, who had been meticulously cared for by my grandparents, it was even more difficult. My “scream” was the shower on the first night in the dormitory. And the second shower inside a dormitory would be postponed until the night of September 11, 2023, about seven years later. The story branches in two; let us tell one at a time. Living in the dorm for five consecutive days in one go, without showering, brushing teeth, or washing one’s face, anyone would stink to high heaven—this seems normal? But setting aside words of symbolic meaning, that vividly lifelike action of my classmate—approaching me, nostrils flaring, hastily retreating, left hand fanning the air—“Eww, so smelly!”, was a heavy blow to me in the sense of pre-symbolic language. I read the pre-symbolic, while he perhaps merely expressed the symbolic. This is perhaps the reason I refuse to output pre-symbolic language. The past me was quite active on social media platforms, but after being called inconsistent between my outer and inner selves by classmates, I began to lean towards silence on social media platforms, silence, silence in all places.

If you can spin a cocoon to bind yourself, you can break out of the cocoon and become a butterfly. I have already spun a cocoon to bind myself, yet I have still not broken out to become a butterfly.

My love for programming still began with that blue Easy Programming Language tutorial in elementary school. She was definitely the thickest and heaviest book I owned at the time. Although the contents have long faded from memory, the fact that the simple virus I wrote in Easy Programming Language was believed to be real still makes me happy whenever I think about it up to this day. Fast forward to middle school, I heard about competitive programming, and began to teach myself for it. I should still be able to find the code left over from teaching myself programming in January 2019; at that time oj.noi.cn was still accessible, and I must have ground through dozens of problems on it—though far fewer than the four hundred plus problems I ground through during the summer after my senior year of high school, but, after all, the high school entrance exam was imminent back then. My worn-out, truly worn-out copy of Beginning Algorithm Contests (The Discouragement Classic), with its Tsinghua-purple cover, was a treasure I couldn’t put down even during summer camp. Even on the bus ride home on Fridays, I was still mentally executing the code from that book in my mind. I truly loved her so much.

The Master said: “To learn alone and without friends makes one solitary, uncultivated, and of narrow hearing.” Pure self-study was ultimately of limited help to me. Lacking a teacher’s guidance, before I participated in NOIp for the first time in my first year of high school, I didn’t even know there was such a thing as a preliminary round that was purely a written test without touching a computer. Thus, with a ranking of 1500/3000, I was eliminated without even entering the Senior Division final round. Thinking about it now, I really should have registered for the Junior Division. However, my homeroom teacher and the IT teacher clearly didn’t know the gap between my level and the level required by the competition either. In a small town, not only the test-grinders, but even the teachers, suffer from the information gap.

Shortly after that, I was hospitalized for two weeks due to depression. Then, medical leave, for a year. I still feel that my homeroom teacher in the tenth grade, Class of 2019, was the best teacher I have ever met. Coming back from the leave of absence, there is even less to say: self-harm, attempted suicide, going home, returning to school, self-harm, aborted suicide, going home, returning to school… this cycle repeated for a long time before it stopped. This period coincided with my father’s death; my mother was deeply grieved, to the point of madness. It practically formed a negative feedback loop with me. A total mess. Come to think of it, a certain nurse pityingly believed that the growth rings of dozens of cuts on my arm were perhaps, objectively speaking, still a manifestation of my firm willpower. I seemed to accept her statement at the bottom of my heart. I consider myself to be of firm willpower. But this ought to have nothing to do with the fact that I didn’t cry at my father’s funeral.

The opening ceremony a few days ago should be the second large-scale occasion where I publicly wore arm sleeves; the first should have been wearing the class uniform, taking graduation photos. During the several years from then until this moment, with scars on my arm, I have always worn long sleeves and long pants. In the summer, aside from being slightly hot, what’s so strange about it—it’s super cool, okay?

Next, let us look to the future. I have an incomparably urgent desire to change my major, to enter Computer Science; my entire summer’s preparation was for this, my goal since childhood has been for this, and my not choosing physics—thereby losing the right to choose almost all engineering majors—was caused by the information gap between my teachers and me, as well as my nonchalant or perhaps overly trusting mindset. But it is not too late. If possible, I would still like to set my lifelong career in computers and calligraphy. Although the latter is currently limited to hard-tipped pens. Yet for me to set such goals right now inevitably carries the suspicion of being naive.

I have no fear of the challenges of knowledge in a world composed of electronic circuits, and I am willing to meet them with my consistent effort from the past, aiming for a guaranteed postgraduate recommendation to Zhejiang University. This answer is bound to be in the style of my age—naive and unsettled.

As for career planning, no one can give a textbook-format answer before actually studying, and my simple, unadorned answer is a developer. I love that wonderful world composed of lines and lines of code. One night, it occurred to me that each of those programs that run perfectly after compilation is practically my proud child; I love her so much.

I am no longer willing to change myself, to cater to others. I seem to have understood that famous quote by Hemingway, though the phrasing I prefer is, “A man can be destroyed, can be defeated, but cannot be changed.”

May my “comfort zone” expand evermore.

entry.title: The Origin of Sovereignty, A Book Report on *The Social Contract*
entry.content:
The Origin of Sovereignty — A Book Report on The Social Contract

The Social Contract (also translated into Chinese as Min Yue Lun), is a great work written in 1762 by the Franco-Swiss thinker Jean-Jacques Rousseau.

Rousseau was one of the great thinkers of the 18th-century French Enlightenment. One of his most famous masterpieces, The Social Contract, provided, to a certain extent, programmatic theoretical guidance for the formulation of the French and American constitutions. Rousseau’s views played a positive driving role during the Enlightenment, yet they still possess the inherent limitations of his bourgeois class nature. Their ultimate aim is to preserve bourgeois rights such as liberty and equality, rather than proceeding from the fundamental standpoint of the broader, neglected grassroots masses of a socialist nature. This is worthy of critical reflection.

In Book I, first of all, Rousseau depicts with exquisite and concise prose the possibility of why the social contract exists. Arguing from the perspective of the source of power, Rousseau negates the views of Grotius and Hobbes, which lean more toward the natural existence of rulers (p. 6). By pointing out the miserable plight of slaves in a slave society, and using vivid examples, he proves by contradiction the absurdity of slaves giving themselves away gratuitously, thereby denying that force is a sufficient condition for right. Since neither power nor right can be derived from force, and most certainly do not arise from nature (p. 4), whence, then, do the rights of rulers come? Through this interrogation, Rousseau introduces the concept of the social contract: namely, that “men have reached the point at which the obstacles in the way of their preservation in the state of nature show their power of resistance to be greater than the resources at the disposal of each individual for his maintenance in that state (p. 18).” To this end, people must find a form of association—namely, the social contract. Rousseau believes this is the genesis of the so-called confederation or republic. In Chapter 7 and beyond, Rousseau mainly discusses the means of maintaining the social contract after its creation: the force of the Sovereign, and finally points out the feasibility of the social contract on a utilitarian level.

In Book II, building upon the genesis of sovereignty in Book I, Rousseau explores the nature of sovereignty—such as its inalienability, its indivisibility, and its limits—as well as what I consider to be the form through which sovereignty functions within a state: the law. For instance, Rousseau’s assertion that “seeing that the law unites universality of will with universality of object… it is not an act of sovereignty, but of magistracy. (pp. 47-48)” points out that sovereignty, as the collective will of the citizens, originates from all citizens, and out of justice, its object is likewise the entirety of the citizenry. However, it is worth noting that Rousseau’s own limitations as a bourgeois thinker are also glimpsed in this book: Rousseau subjectively divides civilizations into periods of so-called “youth” and “childhood,” and further believes that civilizations, or nations, in their so-called youth cannot “recover their liberty,” but can only gradually ossify—much like the decaying tracks of the thousand-year Roman Empire and the barbarism beneath the iron hooves of the Russian Empire. He also argues that in a vast nation, “not only has the government less vigour and promptitude for securing the observance of the laws, preventing nuisances, correcting abuses, and guarding against seditious undertakings begun in distant places… it also has less affection.” (p. 60), and thus must inevitably disintegrate from within. Yet, without a doubt, China in the New Era—a magnificent and vast country—and the Chinese nation in the New Era, brimming with vitality, have thoroughly cast off the thousand-year-old feudal system. Holding high the great banner of the system of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics, they are marching on the great Long March of the New Era; scientific socialism and ancient China are radiating the freedom and vitality of youth in the East of the 21st century. The superior system, the outstanding leadership of the Communist Party of China, and the great achievements China has made serve as powerful evidence falsifying this view of Rousseau’s.

In Book III, Rousseau first utilizes the distinction between legislative power and executive power to achieve the separation of the Sovereign—the people—and the Government—the agent of public force. The Sovereign grants power to the government, and the Sovereign’s power derives from the people, which I personally believe is akin to both the People’s Congress and the People’s Government in our country. When discussing the classification of governments, Rousseau classically divides them into monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy; however, views such as the vitality of a government being negatively correlated with the number of magistrates are obviously erroneous. This error lies in Rousseau’s bourgeois nature, which makes him naturally regard the masses as ignorant—a manifestation of elitist rule. Moreover, Rousseau could never have imagined that the system of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics would make true democracy possible: “If we take the term in the strict sense, there never has been a real democracy, and there never will be… It is unimaginable that the people should remain continually assembled to devote their time to public affairs…” (p. 84). The system of People’s Congresses and the principle of democratic centralism truly represent the fundamental interests of the broadest masses of the people. Beyond this, however, the requirements for a good government pointed out by Rousseau are still worthy of reference for our country’s social governance today—even if there is no absolute standard for a so-called good government—“Subjects extol public tranquillity, citizens individual liberty; the one class prefers security of possessions, the other that of person” (p. 106). Perhaps Socialism with Chinese Characteristics can resolve this seemingly conflicting dilemma. Rousseau’s reverence for the rule of law and the sanctity of legislative power—“The State subsists by means not of the laws, but of the legislative power.” (p. 113)—may hold positive reference value for building a law-based China characterized by good laws and good governance.

In Book IV, Rousseau first approaches from a concrete level to discuss the various details of government and the various ways of maintaining the rights of the Sovereign and the stability of the state. However, I cannot agree with his subsequent exposition on the importance of religion. Even though the thousand-year history of wars and annexations in the ancient West can almost entirely be viewed as a history of struggles between religions, with one taking the stage no sooner than another steps down. “By means of this holy, sublime, and true religion… that society would not dissolve even unto death.” (p. 175), yet the reality of Chinese society is vastly different from this, having nothing whatsoever to do with what Rousseau calls Christianity. Perhaps this is because the common ideal of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics and the lofty ideal of Communism serve as the shared goals of the Chinese people, enabling the great, glorious, and heroic Chinese people to strive ceaselessly.

In terms of writing style, I find that Rousseau vividly employs methods including examples, citations, and numerical calculations to make his arguments—such as calculating the ratio between magistrates and the people; pointing out the respective goals of Carthage, Tyre, and Rhodes in their eras; and citing the views of past sages like Grotius and Aristotle to either critique or endorse them. Drawing extensively from diverse sources and handling complex topics with effortless ease, he demonstrates the superb literacy in political science and jurisprudence possessed by one of the leaders of the Enlightenment. He explains the profound in simple terms, from which I have benefited immensely. At the same time, Rousseau excels at conducting concrete research and discussions on specific countries and specific situations. For example, by pointing out how differences in productivity among various countries lead to different situations of surplus product, as well as the land resources, nature of products, and national customs of each country, he argues that there is no single form of government suitable for all countries. Perhaps the young Marx was also influenced by such a pragmatic, truth-seeking thought of Rousseau’s and carried it forward to greater heights.

In summary, Rousseau’s The Social Contract, as an extraordinarily brilliant work on politics and law, has given me a relatively deeper understanding of the genesis of modern Western democratic systems and their underlying thought, benefiting me a great deal.

entry.title: Step into solitude
entry.content:
Stepping into Solitude

With his battered spine, he snatches my gaze away from a row of vibrant colors; his worn cover seems to lonely proclaim how long he has accompanied me; he casts a cold eye upon the newly arrived, pristine books around him, before retreating alone into the darkness without a word.
I can no longer remember when he came to my side, yet I have toured this kaleidoscopic world over and over again—the borders of the swamp unseen even by the gypsies, the lock of hair slumbering in a reliquary for a hundred years until now, the frigid skyscrapers made of ice and when they might ever be realized from a dream, the intimacy between brothers that gradually vanishes with age, and how the music spilling from the pianola turns sisters into rivals, only for them to grow weary once the prize is won. I cast down my pen, wishing to melt into these thin pages, to swoop past the noisy gasps beneath the eaves on the flying carpet of the first priest from a century ago; I wish to step before the monstrous, shackled man and touch that giant block of ice that refracts the light; I wish to wait with a trembling heart for him to come before me in a bathroom entirely veiled by yellow butterflies and fallen leaves, crawling with scorpions.
My past rebellion was written into the pages as if the author had been standing beside me, observing and gazing closely, as though the loneliness I had experienced before—the loneliness of growing up—were a performance staged according to his script. Like that girl, I played a piano described only in ideals, displaying my excellence and brilliance before others, yet never for a single second of my life stepping away from the grandmother who represented shelter, who sheltered me. Yet on a night that could not have been more ordinary, destroying all the honors I had gained simply for the sake of destruction, with scorpions and spiders surrounding my unshielded, trembling, naked body, I welcomed a purpose that had already been killed by a shotgun. Although, in the novel, after the only surviving infant was sent away in a bamboo basket upon the water, she was sent off and forced to tragically end her tragic, lonely life alone in a tomb-like convent, I felt awakened by this story, quickly breaking free from my own rebellion and smiling bitterly at my own growth.
My fervor was taught to me by José Arcadio Buendía. To successfully promote his somniloquy-like solar warfare, he was willing to travel thousands of miles to a capital that was impossible to reach at the time! When I sink into the swamp of unsolvable math problems, he guides me forward with an absolutely optimistic spirit that fills heaven and earth. My composure is the gloomy mist of Old Melquíades; with his hat like a black crow, he etched a deep memory into my heart.
With more than ten minutes left before six o’clock in the morning, I used to sit alone in my seat with my beloved book, secretly savoring that deserted, tranquil dawn that seemed to exist outside of time, until the space of the classroom that belonged to me alone was stripped away by the growing clamor of arriving people. Embracing him, I overcame the nervousness in my heart and walked through the bustling crowds, as if sheltered by him and unnoticed by anyone. I have copied down countless excerpts from One Hundred Years of Solitude—those sentences that seemed to strike a profound resonance in the depths of my soul, that lonely wandering of ghosts in the rain, and that swamp stretching to the other side of the world, all made me linger.
Time presses heavily upon me. Stepping into solitude, the end of solitude is naturally growth. Aureliano believed that the function of money was nothing more than a tool to gild keys. He could hardly feel the slightest resonance with any potential use of money, devoting everything instead to the alchemy he so dearly loved, just as I use electronic devices to search for problems to improve myself rather than indulging in meaningless feeds of information or deeply despised games. Or like the fifth-generation Aureliano, locking himself in that ancient room forgotten by people for far, far too long, where only the sunlight through the window lattice remained a constant guest, throwing his energy into studying the parchments to the point of forgetting food and sleep—just like my own uncontrollable passion for immersing myself in problems in the small hours of the night. And Melquíades’s fervent goodwill in repairing the pianola, a goodwill like that of an innocent child disregarding reality and trying with all his might to apply his ancient wisdom, touched me so deeply.
Most famous of all is the Colonel who won renown in the wars, even though most people take greater delight in talking about the countless assassination attempts he survived, or the exquisite, handcrafted little goldfishes sold after the war that people so longed to possess. He represents aloofness and ambition, bearing a dual name, yet his most unforgettable achievement was truly looking at and remembering the appearance of his aging mother for the first time. That mother with a mouthful of rotting teeth, a head of white hair, and frightened eyes—while he searched his deepest, most distant memories for a matching image, only to find he no longer possessed any warm memories. For a long time, I dared not look anyone directly in the eye, letting my evasive gaze rest frantically on the lapels of others, as if I were looking at them. Yet, I am fortunate enough to face a mother who has not yet grown old, to adorn the room with the swooping and melodious cooing of white doves alongside her on some late-rising morning as fresh as those in the book. Many years later, I will surely remember that beautiful morning, when youth like the rising sun sparkled in my mother’s eyes.
Even though the family condemned to one hundred years of solitude will not have a second opportunity on earth, is everything in life already predestined? Even though death had already struck as a shadow in the Colonel’s childhood, were not the victories he won time and again spoken of time and again a hundred years later? When I close the pages, countless yellow butterflies once again flutter in my mind; when the Colonel turns his past experiences into verses and rhymes, when in the corridor of begonias he once again sees his family as if resurrected from distant memories, his solitude has quietly shattered into yellow butterflies. When stepping into solitude, we will encounter tens of thousands of different sorrows, yet in the end, we shall not be trapped in the mist.

Written for a certain essay contest

entry.title: Growth and Solitude
entry.content:
Solitude is tearing up books in class, while the teacher turns a blind eye;
Solitude is a late-night heart-to-heart with an unsheathed utility knife;
Solitude is the countless hesitations behind the railing of a windowsill;
Solitude is the bitter medicinal powder, barely swallowed down with thick yogurt;
Solitude is treading upon the evening glow, walking past a thousand newly-lit lamps, and stepping into the nether gloom;
Solitude is the drafts upon drafts of suicide notes piling up in the drawer;
Solitude is going to the cafeteria alone, day after day;
Solitude is weeping, begging your parents to spare you;
Solitude is the torrential downpour that drenches you.

Growth is born in the depths of solitude; he makes solitude understand just how insignificant others are.
Growth shatters the glass bottle brimming with tears, savors the peeled-off scabs, and tells solitude:
Only you are inseparable from yourself, bound to fulfill your own yearnings, born on the selfsame day and dying on the selfsame day, knowing each other’s every thought.
Growth is living, while solitude is ceaselessly thinking of dying the very next moment.
I hold tightly to my past self, while the future leaves not a single trace.
Embracing the golden setting sun, growth pulls solitude—shrouded entirely in a haze of bleakness and sorrow—up from the black mire, only to watch, powerless, as solitude wrenches free from his hands.

Just an assigned prose piece the teacher asked for after we studied “One Hundred Years of Solitude”, I suppose
