entry.title: In the counseling room
entry.content:
In the Counseling Room

Today’s visitor is a boy. The moment he sat down, his very first words startled me
“I am afraid of all teachers.”
What kind of boy is this?

During this hour meant for class, why would he come here to me instead of attending his lesson?
And why do the sounds of shoes treading the sports ground and PE teachers calling the roll drift continuously through the window? Like background music, it served to better explain what the boy was going through.

Afterward, he answered nothing at all. He just stared and stared at my shoes to the point where I felt embarrassed. After I flipped the hourglass, his attention seemed to fixate entirely upon it—anything to avoid looking into my eyes. Not once did he look me in the eye.

He also said that after all this time, he couldn’t even clearly remember what his classmates looked like, because he didn’t dare look at their faces. And the reason he didn’t dare look at their faces was that when you look at someone’s face, you inevitably look into their eyes first—look into their eyes! Heavens, he lamented so, yet I cannot see others’ eyes clearly at all. My eyes are nothing but a murky chaos, my pupils merely a monotonous brown; I have nothing. I do not have fair skin, I cannot write a neat hand, I do not have a pleasant voice.

Really? he said.

He still remembers with crystal clarity the few people who had praised his voice, treasuring those fond memories like a sweet spring, locked away to be recalled only on occasion, whereupon they tasted as sweet as aged nectar.
The first was in seventh grade, when he mustered the courage to share a reading at the podium for the first time. To the girls who had not heard him speak a word several weeks into the semester, the voice of this introverted boy was nothing short of a mystery. Later, online, he was told that his voice was lovely—an anonymous message from a girl in his class who herself had a lovely voice.

The second time was his ninth-grade science teacher. He was very young, and another aspect of his youth that the boy admired immensely was how he spoke frankly before the whole class about the injustices he had suffered at the school, openly confessing his thoughts of dying and of resigning. The boy felt that a man like this was far more sincere than all those other hypocritical teachers. Toward all the other teachers, even those who treated him kindly, he harbored an inexplicable fear. At the time, the teacher called on him to answer a question, and afterward smiled with genuine surprise, saying, so your voice is this pleasant to hear. He sat down silently and said nothing, yet at that moment, he was truly, truly happy.

The third time was during a summer camp in eighth grade, on the journey back to school after it ended. He sat next to the most outstanding girl in the school. She had simply noticed there were no seats left in the back while the one beside him was empty, so she sat down right next to the boy, entirely free of the habit shared by other boys and girls of never sitting with the opposite sex. She shared her potato chips with him; he only dared take one piece at a time, his hand trembling each time he reached out. She praised how nice his voice sounded, yet he foolishly tried to explain why his voice sounded nice—if you never speak, your voice naturally becomes nice.

Since then, he never again heard anyone praise his voice, because he stopped speaking altogether, to the point where quite a few strangers wondered if he were mute. He always wore a gloomy face. Occasionally he was indeed in a foul mood, yet even when his spirits were high, he would still over-manage his expressions—a fact evident from how he would hold back his laughter upon hearing a dirty joke, only to be caught holding it back countless times.

His father passed away very early on, which was routinely assumed to be the cause of his illness. Yet he repeatedly emphasized that he did not care in the slightest about his father’s death, so much so that his family thought him cold, heartless, and incapable of loving anyone. Still, he said his father was an incredible man, because he had successfully quit smoking for his mother’s sake.

He said he was truly afraid of teachers.

Yet upon my questioning, he added: You are pretty nice, though.

I smiled.

He seemed to deeply hope that I could change his life at school. Only then did I notice that even though the wind outside was bone-chillingly cold, as if on the verge of snowing, he was still wearing his autumn school uniform rather than a winter padded jacket.

Why are you dressed like this? Are you cold?

He said that on his way to this building, the wind blew so hard it made him cry. He felt as though every part of his body had been snatched away by the cold wind, leaving him entirely out of control. He felt an endless agony spreading through every inch of his body, as if the freezing wind were about to dismember him. He struggled with all his might to hug himself, yet could only shed a few tears.

Then why not wear something thicker? The school should have issued winter padded jackets, right?

Because that would be so strange! he said. Isn’t putting on the winter uniform an utterly strange thing to do? Just as strange as wearing a padded jacket in the summer—though obviously, wearing shorts in the summer is also a strange, incomprehensible behavior.

In what way is that strange at all? I truly couldn’t quite understand.

I don’t understand myself very well either. Yet the only words I can think of are strange, or out of place, and my brain really hasn’t told me why it is strange. Thus he spoke.

Do you know how cold I am during the winter in the dormitory? Do you know how, because of my father’s carelessness, after my mattress was mistaken for a duvet cover, how narrow and cramped my quilt became how freezing how helpless in the icy night keeping me from falling asleep?
I curled myself up tightly with all my strength, spreading the narrow quilt half beneath me and half over me, clutching my thighs tightly like an infant, while trying my best to avoid any further unstable contact with the quilt. Because the quilt was simply made of ice, as freezing as trouser legs in winter. I was so cold I was about to cry again. Yet not a single person noticed my coldness that day; everyone treated my silence as just as ordinary as on any other day. I found that rather absurd, really.

I wanted to give him a hug, but his body was somewhat stiff.

He said he wasn’t used to hugging others, that it made him feel an inexplicable fear.

entry.title: Lute of the Heart
entry.content:
The Heart-Zither

The river flowed like icy glass.
Artienbu dismounted to the ground; the boundless expanse of water seemed to stretch into another world.
The banks were carpeted with pale flowers that seemed one with the river, like a universe of tiny white blossoms, almost entirely obscuring the pale yellow path.
Artienbu gazed across the river. Save for the pale clouds silently wheeling, save for the startled birds suddenly skimming past, save for the fishing boats lost decades ago now drifting astray in a distant, dreamlike realm, Artienbu could see nothing at all.
He saw only a vastness of pale white, a vastness of pale white, a vastness of pale white.

Downstream towered two white mountains facing each other, with clouds coiling around them like white silk ribbons. Nestled between the peaks was a tiny wooden cabin—the only yellow in a sea of cold hues, the only touch of warmth.
Artienbu turned back in silence. The path behind him led from a colossal green forest that stretched to distant emerald mountains. That was whence he came, having forsaken his homeland and cast aside his noble status as a prince, all in search of that instrument at the end of the world, spoken of in books and by the aged magician on his deathbed—the Heart-Zither (Heart of Piano). The melodies she played were beyond compare, far surpassing even Lüqi, the prized zither of the East immortalized in the verses of bards. Setting aside poetic hyperbole, the Heart-Zither was the one true instrument capable of healing all maladies. When the Heart-Zither is struck by a musician of pure white, the sun and the moon shall rise together in the East.

Artienbu sank into his memories.
Since the deaths of his sister and mother, his solitude had endured to this very day.

His mother died upon that vast, golden wheat field, where she had been standing with her people, counting the bountiful harvest in the autumn wind. Then the daylight faded, and on a gloomy, moonless night, she vanished without a trace from the royal carriage built expressly for her. Had the two coachmen not sworn time and again that they truly did not see how the Queen disappeared into that gust of wind, they would both have been beheaded.

His sister’s favorite place was the royal library. Amidst the dim aisles flanked by mountains of books, one could spot the little girl in her resplendent gown. Her figure and braids cast ever-swaying shadows in the lamplight, and her eyes gleamed like a cat’s in the dark. On the cover of the book cradled in her arms, the expression of the long-dead historian seemed to shift gradually from calm, to astonishment, to madness.
His sister would find a wine cask somewhere in the library, sit atop it, and begin to read by the dancing lamplight mounted upon the marble walls engraved with royal crests.
Artienbu would occasionally play hide-and-seek with his sister in the library.
Until one day, when Artienbu went to the library at dawn as usual to find his sister, who had stayed there through the night to rest, she had vanished without a trace.
The God of Strength carved upon the marble door swore that he could still feel her breath lingering within the library, and the candles bowed their heads uneasily to Artienbu to profess their loyalty, yet none of this could undo the truth that his sister was gone.
What manner of power could it possibly be?
Artienbu breathed a long sigh toward the East; his eyes caused the very sun to summon thick clouds and mist to veil itself.

The soul doth hide within the due East, the soul is ever fond of the Sun, the soul is wrought of malted gold, for only thus may it endure the Sun’s resplendent light
The soul doth hide within the West, the soul chants of autumn leaves that wither and fade to gold, the soul stands at the broken end of time, counting with care the solitude and sorrow of the years untold
The soul doth hide within the North, the soul melds with the drifting snow and wind across the sky, the soul becomes the vast expanse of peak and stream, the soul delights in all the world’s cold frost, the soul admires all life’s pale, bewildered sigh
The soul doth hide within the South, that it might draw more nigh the blazing Sun, that it might rove the boundless Southern heaven and earth, that the deep wishes of the land be done

The soul doth slumber in the central place.

entry.title: Yi'an's Anthology of Verses and Lyrics
entry.content:
Phoenix Perching on the Parasol Tree

Since parting from Zhaoyang, I waste away apace;
Cold stands the silver screen, fierce winds shatter the flute’s grace.
Looking back, the clepsydra shifts, the waning moon sinks low;
Through the endless night, in vain I face the red candle’s glow.

Sleet and snow seal the heavens, the chill doth not retreat;
Rain-bells ring in the courtyard, frost-laden winds invade my sheet.
Though I don every silken robe, how can autumn yet remain?
A hundred years of wind and snow—a boundless sea of pain.

Untitled

The autumn wind sweeps down the parasol leaves; upon the steps, whose heart is rent and grieves?
Wiping from both cheeks the tears of many a day, in silent sorrow I pine and waste away.
O’er distant peaks, the migrating geese are bound to pass; falling leaves and autumn sounds ride the ceaseless blast.
The whirling autumn wind carpets the ground in gold; alone I lean by the withered well, 'midst winds vast and cold.
The dim fire of my sorrow flickers, nigh to die; the four walls stand desolate, as if steeped in moonlight from the sky.
The geese skimming past the western tower know me not; once parted, when shall our acquaintance be re-wrought?
My remnant soul in the waning night sees dreams congeal and fade; speechless I sit in silence till the dawn is made.

Untitled

A wan crescent moon approaches my casement pane; frost climbs the jasper mirror, the night is icy and vain.
The wind bullies the candle flame, rain falls in a thousand lines; in an empty chamber I hang myself, facing the stark white wall’s confines.

II

The frosty moon knits its brows, peering through the casement old; chill invades the jade mirror, the night is vast and cold.
The wind rends the remnant candle, tears fall in a thousand lines; a lone shadow hangs from the beam, facing the pale wall’s confines.

Butterflies Lingering o’er Flowers

Red leaves cover my robes, the wind fills the ground; sweeping away the autumn sounds, no fragrant letter is found.
Vast and dreary, a light chill seals the sky’s hue; in misty, gauzy rain, the heavens weep anew.
Graceful characters on painted stationery lay old memories bare; the night is dark and estranged—whence rises this despair?
The pond steeps the Three Stars deep within cloud and mist; a hooked, slumbering moon therein doth rest and tryst.

II

Red leaves brush my robes, the wind fills the stone stair; idly chasing autumn sounds, in vain I wait for word from the clouds’ lair.
Vast and dreary, a light chill—the sky grows dim andоз; misty rain weaves a thousand threads of woes.
Colored ink on fine stationery folds memories of yore; the night is dark and blurring, cold dew soaks my lapel to the core.
The pond steeps the Three Stars, their light shimmering chill; half a curved toad-moon slumbers in the wave’s heart still.

Untitled

At dusk, yellow flowers in the evening light剪 (silhouette) a figure lone; river winds blow my sleeves, the water adds a trace of its own.
With the netherworld filling my boat, return I cannot make; o’er distant hills, a crescent moon bids forest whispers wake.

Dreaming of Jiangnan

Idle dreams drift far; in the northern realm, early winter hath begun.
Waters merge with the sky in a thousand leagues of jade; reed-blossoms mourn in the rain and the cold wind’s run.
One rises 'midst the bright moon’s sheen.

Sands of the Washing Stream

Several bends of vermilion walls encircle the rustic vill;
Jade moss brims the steps and creeps toward the portal sill;
Spring winds lock the courtyard deep and still.

Fine rain and gentle breezes blow the grasses green;
Flowing reed-pipes mix with tears, enduring a soul-rending scene;
By the deserted pond I stand alone, where rain falls keen.

Untitled Seven-Character Regulated Verse

The wind crushes remnant leaves to fall on the deserted vill; waves rock a lonely boat, its lantern flickering chill.
Dark and cold, a thousand peaks are splashed with heavy ink; somber and serene, twixt two realms, faint traces link.
Rippling waters cradle a sunken crescent moon; faint thunder rumbles, shattering my dream-soul’s swoon.
In the autumn rain of Jiangnan, upon a turret small, through the cool night I drink alone—warm must the wine-cup fall.

II

The wind crushes withered leaves that knock the brushwood door; waves beat the fishing lamp, the reed-marsh dims o’er.
In ten thousand ravines, pine-waves churn in hues of ink; across the whole river, threads of rain embroider the mossy brink.
Bobbing and sinking, the cold moon-hook seems to weep; flickering, startling thunder threatens to swallow the night deep.
Alone I lean in the lofty tower, hearing a flute’s broken strain; warming a pot of chrysanthemum wine, with autumn IHold converse in vain.

Southerner’s Song

Fine rain falls in a misty dream; scattered icy dust by white fog is crushed andgleamed.
Beyond the heavens, a shooting star skims the horizon’s rim; by the courtyard door, another year passes, and he returns not to the dim.
Silently the moon hangs low; pillow and mat congeal with frost, frost climbs my brow of woe.
Tossing and turning, sleepless, my tears waste me away; the wind blows—all o’er the ground, shattered jade cups and琉璃 (glaze) lay.

Southerner’s Song

The hue of rain grows blurred and lost; in the quiet, fragrant courtyard, I hark to the birds’ plaintiveost.
Jade moss invades the steps, the door is half-ajar; in sorrow, the wind weeps o’er grieving blossoms unwilling to depart afar.
Silent the rain, swallows fly in a pair; alone I stand by cold waves, drinking a cup of snow-filled air.
Mists assail the distant hills, the sky prepares to close; the reed-organ plays—how many times have I asked if my lord returns or goes?

Untitled

White dew spans the heavens, the autumn wind is spent; flying snow fills the city, veiling the bright moon’s ascent.
Shaking down a thousand lamps, the netherworld draws nigh; teeth chatter, bones freeze, my spirit is rent with a sigh.
In the evening sky, faint and far, the crows’ cries fade; in the languid night, cicadas chirp in mournful serenade.
Alone I sit on ancient steps as fleeting scenes glide past; withered trees and I keep vigil through the eternal night vast.

Sands of the Washing Stream

Gradually the icy wind, gradually grows chill;
Along the sunset path, alone I wander still.
Behind theclustering blossoms stands a lofty wall on the hill.

A single swimming fish roams free and unrestrained;
Ten thousand tangled thoughts are all with sorrow stained.
High in the perilous tower I lean, where the north wind rages unchained.

Untitled

Over bitter wine I recall the days of yore;
Cold the sand, bright the moon’s lore.
Across the heavens, the scenery is studded with stars galore;
Snow falls on the little bridge, plum blossoms dot the view, o’er the river the wind is pure.

Alone, tilt not the goblet deep;
Who will listen to the secrets I keep?
Through the passing years, my journey to the Jasper Garden was ne’er made.
From a shallow, drifting dream, who would wish to wake, worn and sorrow-weighed?

Untitled

Ten leagues of icy wind lock the frigid river’s flow; gazing o’er my native streams, the evening rain is vast and low.
A lean horse and short robe gallop down the ancient way; o’er distant peaks, a solitary wild goose chases the dying day.

Untitled

Forsaken in the Silver River, the stars tremble in fright; the north wind shakes the琉璃 (crystal) goblets through the night.
A cloud-cleaving sickle moon reflects on the tower cold; all night long, sharp reed-pipes sever the soul from its hold.
With snow filling the river’s heart, how can peace be found? Mists churn beyond the mountains, my heart in chaos bound.
Boundless night rain begins to murmur and weep; in several places, the cuckoo’s cry shatters dreams from sleep.

II

The Silver River freezes and cracks, stars like scabs congeal; the north wind licks up every shattered crystal-meal.
A broken moon slits the throat, the clouds weep gore; a desolate flute tears the lungs, its voice rasping and sore.
River snow swallows the boat, bones sink to the bed; mountain mist coils round the neck, a knotted rope’s scar red.
A dying lamp bites through the flesh of midnight’s gloom; withered branches snap their waists, heaven and earth are struck dumb in doom.

Butterflies Lingering o’er Flowers

True cultivation hath ne’er crowned our schooling’s name;
Exam-bound it remains, where scores are all the game.
Day by day at desks they speak of easing the load; year by year, extra lessons waste winter and summer on this road.

Schoolwork piles like mountains, joy returns no more;
In vain my colored brush writes, dreaming of childhood paths of yore.
Alone I stand in the lake’s heart, the wind veils my eyes; a shooting star across the horizon finds no place to rise.

The Phoenix Hairpin

Flowers beyond count, yet where art thou? In gloom I turn my head at twilight’s brow.
A place of broken heart, hard to stay my pace; a small boat drifts afar, the moon loses the ford’s trace.
Stars dance.

Wind-bells chime,青衣 (dark robes) rise; in the painted tower I hear all the plum-rain’s sighs.
The wind looks back, mountains coil in mist; swallows startle in courtyard trees, tears hide where remnant rains persist.
Alone I stand.

II

Willows droop by the ford, blossoms leave the tree; the traveler’s boat rocks and shatters the sunset on the sea.
The wind seems to訴 (complain), one can hardly stay; half a river of misty waters, a lapel full of flying catkins gray.
Wrong. Wrong. Wrong.

Eave-bells speak, yellow plum-rain falls; embroidered curtains roll up in vain as spring’s trace leaves the halls.
Clouds block the road, swallows startle in the wood; the bright moon of yesteryear shatters into cold dew where it stood.
I look back. Look back. Look back.

III

Evening clouds cross the ford, misty shoals and trees; leaning on the balustrade, I gaze back at the sunset’s breeze.
My青衫 (blue robe) was a mistake, the magnolia oar departs; half a river of cold jade, several peaks wrapped in misty arts.
I linger. Linger. Linger.

Eave-bells speak, yellow plum-rain falls; the painted tower locks in vain the aloeswood incense within its walls.
The wind startles the egret, sorrow is like catkins spun; moss invades the stone tablet, tears drown theunfinished verse begun.
I peer. I peer. I peer.

The Phoenix Hairpin

The stars are in turmoil, dust on the rafters is dim; the north wind shakes the crystal cup to its brim.
I gaze at my lone shadow, facing the mirror of bronze; in the river’s heart the moon melts, my dream seeks secluded fronds.
Ill. Ill. Ill.

That flower-like face, long unseen; on emerald mountains spring withers, clouds refuse to leave the scene.
Fleeting scenes fly past, sorrow is eternal; blue wings perch on the parasol tree, green and red are buried on paths vernal.
Fate. Fate. Fate.

Southern Song

Water-sleeves rise with a chilly grace,
Rouge tinting a faint crimson trace.
Leaning along every balustrade, with swallows I meet;
Across the courtyard, willow-catkins fly, weeping all their tears in the spring wind fleet.

Fingers grow cold, flute and reed-pipe fade afar;
Deep in the cup, the amber wine shines like a star.
Misty lamps rock my dreams, my coiled hair-buns come undone;
The morning moon and Three Stars are locked deep where azure clouds run.

Waves Washing the Sand

Looking back, the moon is chill and clear;
A sea of clouds, an empty city here;
From icy curtains and painted pavilions, a shooting star falls near.
Pointing to the long wind, toward the Silver River I go,
Casting away all that I once held dear.

Master Qu tilts his goblet with me,
Asking what my age might be;
Though past my coming-of-age, to the Jasper Garden I could not flee.
Wind fills my silken robes, my body a swallow in the rain,
Ending this floating life in vanity.

II

Sitting alone, the moon is chill and clear; a lone pavilion hangs with icicles sheer.
The crystal dome of heaven cracks with cold stars’veer.
Fain would I draw the Silver River to wash my weary eyes, shattering the void so bright.
Pouring wine, I ask the netherworld: canst thou endure this lonely plight?
“E’en the immortal maiden weeps upon the jade steps cold.
Let us borrow the mortal world’s hearth-fire hues, to tread the waves and ride the whale bold.”

Remembering the Qin Maiden

The stars shine bright; a lone wolf howls at the moon upon a precipice height.
A precipice height; from willow tips the moon hangs low, an old man fishes in the night.

A melancholic poet seeks verses in the temple hall; painted brows sketch a picture in the fading sunset’s fall.
The fading sunset’s fall; the evening boat turns back its oar, a flute wafts a lingering call.

Waves Washing the Sand

Rustling, the pure breeze; resplendent, the moonlight’s grace.
In the courtyard, an ancient tree gives cold crows a resting place.
Gazing afar at the vast sky, stars are like sleet—flawless jade in space.

Shallow, the traces of tears; flickering, the lamp-wick’s flower.
Jade curtains lightly brush as rain slants down the tower.
Leaning on the rail, I venture to ask: how fares the night? Each at heaven’s far bower.

Spring in the Jade Tower

At dawn I drink alone a heady wine; deep in drunkenness unspent, my frame doth further pine.
Delicate blossoms can scarce endure the heavy, chilling dew; the dragon-brain incense burns out, and my beloved proves untrue.
Through parasol trees, fine rain and gentle breezes go; a courtyard full of withered maple leaves brings unbearable woe.
Dark clouds lose the moon, curtains veil the lamp’s gleam; the long night knows no end, keeping company with the water-clock’s stream.

Sands of the Washing Stream

In the temple, rare incense burns with a幽 (ghostly) flame;
Before the Buddha, I silently chant a ballad to renew our claim:
From this day forth, cast me not into forsaking’s shame.

Maple leaves, clear frost, and the moon at the river’s floor;
A skiff leaves the bank 'midst the driving rain’s roar.
Facing the wind, I stand alone as my tears pour.

Mountain Hawthorn

Fine rain upon the pond, spring grass is sweet;
A gentle breeze caresses the long willow threads’ retreat.
Cries of birds ring out as the wind rolls up the mist;
The rain is vast and indistinct.

Pounding Silk

The wind sighs, right in the depths of spring.
Rain beats the deep portal, the lamp’s shadow is flickering.
Helpless against the long night, I cannot sleep;
Beneath the moon at the latticed window, twin tear-stains creep.

Mulberry-Picking Song

Pear blossoms fill the courtyard as spring departs; a gentle breeze stirs the emerald screen.
A single tune from a flowing reed-pipe
Awakens in whose heart a sorrow keen?

Incense in the burner turns to ash by the curtain-hook’s shadow; good dreams leave no trace behind.
By the marsh’s edge, east of the hedge,
Washed by blazing light, the cherries glow a deeper rind.

Mulberry-Picking Song

A pure breeze blows my dreams to the distant sky; looking back, it adds to my woe.
All before my eyes is waning autumn;
Rustling maple leaves fill the little boat below.

The yellow flowers are thinner even than a rosy face; weary, I lean in the lofty tower’s space.
Nine bends of the frigid stream,
Just like the migrating wild goose that ne’er stays its pace.

Dim Dawn

Dancing fireflies gleam;
The lamp-flower is blown down as the gentle breeze congeals.
The gentle breeze congeals;
Mist confuses the remnant dream, the inky night a light chill feels.

In clear autumn’s icy rain, the bells ring chill and clear;
A sleeping boat’s fishing fire braves the river’s heart near.
The river’s heart near;
Countless streams of flowing silver, a bright moon and myriad stars appear.

II

Dancing fireflies gleam;
The lamp-flower is blown down as cold smoke coils round.
Cold smoke coils round;
Mist confuses the ferry crossing, the oar shatters the bright void’s ground.
Clear frost secretly crosses where bamboo branches chill;
A sleeping boat fishes alone in the vast, dark-blue sea still.
The dark-blue sea still;
A single trace of waning moon, ten thousand scattered stars upon the hill.

Betraying No Emotion

Withered maples fall from the bough’s height; in the mortal realm, naught can stay its flight.
Aloeswood incense burns through the long, rainy night; the autumn moon is pale in the clear autumn light.
Washing roses, fragrant stamens flow with the stream; inscribing stationery, graceful characters sheathe their sharp gleam.
A bright lamp spreads across the desk, gentle and mild, shining bright like thy gaze beguiled.
Mournful cicadas chirp in the courtyard’s secluded keep; tossing waves in the river’s heart rock a boat cold and deep.
Above the light gauze mist hangs a small silver hook; irises fly in pairs, as if on our old excursions’ brook.

Untitled Four-Character Verse

Starry eyes blurred and lost; clouds and moon lean side by side.
A cold wind faintly pierces; the cuckoo softly cries.
Deep, deep the forest path; heavy, heavy my soul’s dream.
My staff catches on dark moss; flickering, the lamp grows dim.

Untitled

Through the window pierces a pure breeze, teasing the red candle into bashful chagrin.
Pale clouds drift; in the vast sky, the moon shines white and thin.
Strolling slowly in the idle courtyard—how many spring blossoms have fallen within?
Quiet, with no one near; dark, secluded, and still the din.

Congealed waves of emerald water; cold dew resents the coming of the dawn.
Hoping for thy return, the aloeswood incense is already gone.
How high are these walls? Moreover, mist confuses the view I would look upon.
Gazing at the azure sky, afar skims the Blue Bird on and on.

Crane Soaring to Heaven

Behind the clouds of the azure sky,
The moon, like a pining lover, grows thin and shy.
Thin mist conceals the fishing pond, a lamp faintly gleams through.
The mountain detains what traveler? The boat is tethered to whose willow view?
The cock’s crow hurries the painted water-clock’s flow;
Alone I lean by the casement window, as if pure wind fills my sleeves with woe.

In dreams I return to the fine rain; with cold fingers, on the jade reed-pipe alone I play.
Thou art like a blossom in the rain, drifting long away.
In the southern courtyard, red petals carpet the ground; northern geese look back in vain.
The west wind wanders everywhere;
The setting sun melts into gold—once more, it is the hour of heartbreak and pain.

Untitled

Alas for the boundless expanse of mist and rain!
Alas for the piercing chill of the whirling gale!
Alas for the broken sorrow of the heavenly moon!
Alas for the soaring flight of the spirit and soul!
Alas for the bewildered gloom of the gathering dusk!
Alas for the mournful cries of the wintering crows!
Alas for the endless stretch of the eternal night!
Alas for the biting frost that covers my bed!
Mournful, alas! Rain and snow fall thick and fast, unsettled and wild.
Sighing, alas! The cold invades my narrow jacket, and I have no robes to wear.
Sorrowful, O! There is no one to walk beside me on my way.
Grieving, alas! The slanting sun sinks into ruin, and I have no home to return to.
Bitter, O! The heart of theFair One is estranged from mine own.
Secluded, O! Bamboo groves bury the spring grass and inter the flowers.
Trembling, O! I can only cover my sleeves and weep all alone.
Desolate, O! I dwell in the bustling market, yet no one knows me.

Eight-Six Measure

Shutting the deep portal, the small tower is caged in rain; through the mist, skimming swallows return from afar again.
By the jade well, sparse parasol trees are climbed by moss; in the empty courtyard, emerald curtains float on the wind’s toss,
Facing the rain, I tilt my cup.

Along the fragrant embankment, willows droop in tender grace.
Beyond the clouds, churning mist locks the hills; in the lake’s heart, shattering waves delay the boat’s pace.
Spring is gone! In the fragrant garden, a hundred flowers are nigh to fade;
Remnant petals are like blood, painted brows remain unswayed.
The wind returns.
Pearl-like tears fall with the oiled umbrella; dark tresses fly with the scattered red blossom-shade.
Beyond the苍 (somber) mountains, ten thousand threads of rosy twilight fade.

Everlasting Longing

Scattered reds fly; cold rain falls fine and shy.
Melancholic, beneath low eaves a pair of swallows return from the sky.
At dusk, the door is half-shut with a sigh.

Pale clouds wheel round; heavy clouds mound.
Hard to limit the bright moon that loses itself in the curtain’s bound.
The west wind hurries the remnant leaves to the ground.

Telling of Innermost Feelings

The sky joins the inky rain to steep the clear autumn scene;
My colored brush drops a sorrow keen.
Frosty winds and tears brim my sleeves; memories can no longer be gathered in.

Thou art gone, the moon cannot stay;
Down sinks the silver hook’s ray.
This life is like a dream; looking back in gloom, the stars resemble thine eyes’ sway.

Short Song

Why do I live?
I shall never know.
I can only see
The forest blotting out the blue sky,
And the sun vanishing from sight.

Untitled

O youths and maidens who have taken your own lives,
You shall keep your youth forevermore.
You are the dancing Spirits of the Valley;
You possess souls of purest white;
You have won the struggle against the world.

Ugly Slave with Added Words

Upon the lightly chilled mat, my silken robes are untied; at midnight I am about to sleep.
At midnight I am about to sleep;
Out the window I suddenly glimpse a sky of pale, vast water-sweep.

The pure breeze rustles as pine branches sway; slender willows bear cotton-down deep.
Slender willows bear cotton-down deep;
Stars steep beside the little bridge, flowing water, and fallen blossoms’ heap.

Sands of the Washing Stream

Three inches of painted stationery lay my yearning bare;
Empty, empty the sea of my heart, white as frost in the air;
Among the woods the rain falls, the mist refuses to clear there.

The plain zither-strings intentionally迷 (bewilder) my dreamland’s plight;
Boundless flying snow buries the flower-terrace from sight.
Threads of gentle light gradually come from the eastern height.

Spring in the Jade Tower

The bright moon ever vexes the sorrowful heart; a startling dream and the cuckoo’s cry find the water-clock still and apart.
Flying blossoms must have fallen west of the turret small; the ground is covered in remnant red, and spring has grown old in the hall.
Phoenix-patterned quilt is chilled as aloeswood smoke curls low; candles warm the painted hall, while the stars shine faint and slow.
A hundred feet of shrimp-whisker blinds rise on silver hooks; the cold moon in heaven’s heart can scarce bring dawn to these nooks.

Sands of the Washing Stream

Rustling river winds rock the little boat; silken robes are helpless against the late autumn’s note.
A light skiff on emerald waters drifts eastward afloat.

Beyond the hills, the setting sun dyes the clouds in gore; along the bank, swaying reeds speak of sorrow’s lore.
By the balustrade, memories can be gathered in no more.

Butterflies Lingering o’er Flowers

A single tune of Yangguan breaks my heart inch by inch;
Alone I lean by the casement window, the moon sinks and remnant clouds flinch.
Forsaken in the Silver River, the stars tremble in fright; the north wind shakes the crystal goblets through the night.

Along the long embankment of emerald willows, the wind grows slow;
On the shimmering lake-light, I think to set a light skiff aglow.
In several places, warbling orioles make spring linger and wind; beneath the leaves by the lofty pavilion, red petals fly unconfined.

Butterflies Lingering o’er Flowers

All night the sparse courtyard endured the nightly rain;
Ten thousand stamens of remnant red, a thousand threads of idle thoughts in vain.
Harsh wine, broken incense, and the wind hurrying by; my robes dance in vain along the Handan road with a sigh.

Jade-carved reed-pipes and flutes speak not a word;
In the distant wilds the sky clears, below the tower the evening sun is blurred.
A waning moon, deep woods, and chilly mist; leaning along every balustrade, in vain I stand and persist.

Seven-Character Quatrain

The azure heavens are vast and boundless, Orion and Scorpio far apart; the clamor upon the streets is even harder to bear in the heart.
The courtyard is secluded and dim, trees and grasses keep silent guard; dew congeals on cold steps, and the evening wind blows hard.

Immortal at the River

Rain accompanies the setting sun, sprinkling the green wilds; the rustling spirit of spring is all too deep.
Delicate poplars and slender willows cannot bear the wind’s sweep.
In light smoke, orchids weep dew; green leaves bury the crimson blossoms’ sleep.

Last night a brocade letter was first delivered here; before opening it, my tears fell like misty rain’s sphere.
Heaven and earth may endure, yet they have their bounds of time and space.
To meet again is naturally impossible—only the cold night and the mountain bell’s grace.

Seven-Character Extended Regulated Verse

Red waves of the quilt are tossed, the golden phoenix grows cold; flying reed-pipes and the morning moon sink by the western tower old.
Rattan bed, paper curtains, and a lightly chilled mat; emerald screens, pearl blinds, and hooks of precious jade flat.
The water-clock stops as daylight climbs to the Ox and Dipper’s height; smoke perfumes the amber wine, diluting my sorrow’s plight.
The cold wind threatens to snuff the small remnant lamp’s gleam; bleak rain is pouring down, bidding my soul’s dream cease its stream.
A thousand catkins fall thick and fast like the bitterness of parting; a lone star shines bright and clear, like thine eyes’ darting.
Outside the jasper window, green willows sway in the breeze; along the winding path of soft mud, butterflies roam in hidden ease.
Last evening we parted ways upon the reed-lined shore; this morning I moor alone a boat that strives against the current’s roar.
Alas, though the colors of spring are infinitely fair, a single fragrant heart is consigned to the wine-tallies there.

Dreaming of Jiangnan

Where art thou, my lord? The misty pavilion resents being long barred.
Pearls of rain tap frequently, throwing the deep candle into disarray; green weeds lock deep the eastern side of the little garden yard.
Overnight, the whole courtyard is strewn with red.

Where art thou, my love? The setting sun and a wine-banner in the wind.
A lone wild goose, cold mountains, and autumn hues stretching far; in travel robes on a lean horse, I stand where the dying sun has thinned.
With tearful eyes, I gaze toward my southern homeland.

Far Return to the Homeland

Thou art gone;
The wind scatters the remnant reds, the setting sun hastens on.
At twilight, boundless is the grief, and sorrows are myriad-drawn.

The Fair One dwells afar within the clouds’ embrace;
Life has reached its evening space.
Where the fragrant grasses join the sky, where is my native place?

Far Return to the Homeland

A traveler in a lonely boat,
Coldly passing a thousand leagues of hills and rivers in a white coat.
A hooked frosty moon parts water and sky afloat.

O’er distant mountains, a single expanse of dim twilight;
The heart of heaven is emerald-bright.
A solitary wild goose, a single speck, flies without a trace in sight.

The Beautiful Lady Yu

Jade curtains and cold rain dissolve my newfound dream;
Against the pillow, the phoenix hairpin is marred in its gleam.
Across a thousand leagues of rivers and hills, the wild geese do not return;
Emerald grass brims the steps, wind-blown catkins fill the sky and churn.

Misty, pale fog locks the vermilion tower tall;
The music of reed-pipes cannot pierce its wall.
This light boat departs, left to drift eastward with the stream;
Vast and boundless, the misty waters hide how many autumns and springs in their dream?

Hundred-Character Lyric

Wind,
Balmy, mild.
Orioles hold red,
Returning swallows in the door.
Light rain sprinkles east of the hedge,
Flutes and songs weave a long rainbow.
In a magnolia boat on clear waters, plucking lotus blooms;
Curling hearth-smoke rises, the sun is warm and one grows languid.
Along the lanes, the blossoms of spring, given by thee, are fairer still;
Crumpling my yellow robe’s threads and tassels, my mood grows misty and blurred.

On a moonlit night, returning to the lofty pavilion, with whom shall I share the view?
In the mirror, my rosy face has already traded its former hue.
A solitary star beyond the heavens resembles the pupil of thine eye;
Clouds pile high and the rain falls misty once more.
Looking back, the candle-flower glows red;
Jade hairpins hold my deepest devotion.
How rich and strong the wine!
Cold maple leaves,
Brief.

Return of Ruan Lang

The lamp dies in the water-palace, revealing the one in my dream;
Languid and weary, the eternal night grows dim.
Roosting crows cry out, breaking the traces of scattered blossoms;
Beneath the bright moon, my soul breaks in vain.

Startled by the urgent rain, resenting the tangled wind;
Fearing the advancing frost, I bar the door within.
Braving the cold, withered leaves harbor a heavy, sinking grief;
After the rain, my sorrow grows deeper beyond relief.

Joy of the Moving Oriole

Wave-shadows sway, leaves drift in yellow flight;
The wind rolls up and hides the moonlight.
In the evening woods, the golden well surges with starlight’s gleam;
Looking back, the mist is vast as a dream.

Soul-melting wine, a rosy face grown thin;
Standing alone, pure wind fills my sleeves within.
My fragrant heart has grown cold, the night is faintly chill;
Before the broken mirror, I bid farewell to my crimson makeup still.

Partridge Sky

Ten leagues of spring wind roll up the blinds for me; seal-script incense burns my dreams as I stand on the morning veranda free.
In the small courtyard of chiming bells, orioles warble in the rain; in the tiered tower of locked regrets, the phoenix brushes the zither’s strain.
Aloeswood smoke curls, the jade goblet stands idle; by the vermilion terrace and jasper mirror, my prime years bridle.
The lamp-flower burns out as the crescent moon ascends; afar I watch the Three Stars circling heaven’s nine bends.

Like a Dream

Heartbroken by the cuckoo’s urgent cry;
Beside the goblet, moths fly and candle-flames dance high.
Chill, chill, a single silver hook above
Shines in vain upon the towers and the ferry-cove.
Listless, listless;
Overnight, whence has the frost sprung forth?

Untitled

One pities the autumn clouds that drift away; the sun sets, yet the evening breeze doth stay.
Only the wrinkled shadows of the pool are seen; unending is my longing, deep and keen.
High the mountains, evening clouds in autumn’s hold; I breathe the sweet fragrance of osmanthus gold.
In the mountain temple, a zither sounds its strain; note after note stirs the drooping willows’ train.
Turbid wine consoles the traveler’s woe; raising my cup, the wind fills my sleeves aglow.

Untitled

Through the long night, the moon is cold and the wind is still; the cuckoo’s cry breaks through, waking me from my dream’s chill.
The curtains are rolled up, pale clouds drift light; in the courtyard, remnant blossoms cast tangled shadows in the night.

A pair of swallows bring fragrant mud along the rainy lane; over a single cup of clear tea, I recall and reflect in vain.
Incense curls like mist, the mat climbs with ice; the jade goblet intoxicates the moon as my eyes first close thrice.

Rouging the Lips

Deep in the twelfth watch of the night,
In the small courtyard of cherry blossoms, one stands long in the light.
The pure breeze wishes to dance;
In an instant, countless petals fly by chance.

The sinking moon is deep in clouds;
I only ask, where art thou in the shrouds?
The cherry blossom tree—
Before the tree, the blossoms fade;
Beneath the tree, one stands long in the shade.

Rouging the Lips

The setting sun and a migrating wild goose;
Clear frost, evening rain, and grass upon the sandy truce.
The frigid river stretches vast and wide;
Leaves scatter down the autumn wind’s wayside.

Ascending the high tower once more,
The moon is waning, the starlight poor.
The jasper cup is overturned;
Longing remains unfulfilled and burned;
In the mirror, a rosy face has aged and mourned.

Seven-Character Regulated Verse

Secret affection and secluded joy—how could they be lightly betrayed? In the rain, a young gallant wanders, withered and frayed.
Myriad stars shine chill, my feelings are hard to tell; the solitary moon lingers fondly, yet the dream does not dwell.
Outside the window, a lean poplar is entwined by the wind’s grace; at midnight, in the cold rain, a traveler paces in place.
Upon the plantain leaves, drop after drop rings clear; gazing up at the azure sky, several lines of tears appear.

Xingdong’s Seven-Character Regulated Verse

In the vermilion tower, behind embroidered blinds, seal-script incense burns low; full of passion, I dare not forget my lord Xiao.
Emerald screens, silver hooks, and painted candles cold; jade mats, golden tripods, and the night rain’s long hold.
Reed-pipes and flutes are speechless, the zither-strings sound bleak; by the Xiao and湘 (Xiang) rivers, there is regret as wild geese wander weak.
Peach-blossom stationery bears my dream in a single letter’s space; pouring out my whole heart, I write in lines of tears’ trace.

Joy of Returning to Court

Churning waves and rolling clouds dim the twilight hue.
Rustling, the cold wind blows as wild geese cry anew.
Along the road, the autumn grass is desolate and bare; where horse-hooves have trodden, no trace remains there.
A wandering traveler from the Three Chu lands;
Thin smoke faintly veils a deserted village post-stand.
Resenting the rustling sound—wind and rain piercing the window-pane, all dripping straight into my heart’s domain.

The frosty moon hangs low, full of tender grace.
In the jade pavilion, by the latticed window, one is lost in memory’s embrace.
Cicadas chirp round the stone steps, never finding peace; beyond the low wall and overgrown path, my gaze finds no release.
In the vault of heaven, ten thousand grains of stars gleam;
Pale clouds come and go, cruelly parting the stream.
Tears follow the wind; standing alone on the mountain crest, a single note rises from a Qiang flute’s breast.

Five-Character Regulated Verse

Moonlight enters the long corridor’s space, filling it bright with white light’s grace.
Footsteps echo in solitary sound; light leaves are left to fly unbound.
My sleeves rise with the wind’s caress; my heart forgets the world’s distress.
Doth the Moon Goddess drink wine tonight? Clear water falls upon my robes so white.

Spring in Wuling

In the courtyard, plantains tint the little path with green; bamboo shoots emerge before the steps’ scene.
A pair of swallows twitter, nesting 'neath the eaves;
Light rain leaps upon the swing’s leaves.

A boat enters the clear-water cove of lotus blooms, gradually waking ripples from their glooms.
A gentle breeze blows the willows, catkins fall upon my shoulder;
In a sea of flowers, butterflies flutter bolder.

Treading on Sedge

Mountains screen green mountains, bordering the lake’s green grass.
A magnolia boat with light oars is ringed by tiny waves that pass.
Among the woods, a traveler of Chu is drunk on blossoms fair; in the tower, pale hands thread the needle with skillful care.

Threads of remnant clouds, the bright moon shines white and clear.
In the endless cold night, the sound of the wind grows still and near.
Tossing beneath the red waves of the quilt, I cannot find sleep; out of nowhere tears arise, for love is too hard to speak or keep.

Immortals at the Magpie Bridge

A single pure song, a whole night of bright moon; on a rattan bed behind paper curtains, sleep comes not soon.
Following the wind, delicate willows sway on their own; where ten thousand lanterns shine, Chang’an cannot bear the groan.
Shooting stars dot the sky, slender clouds drift in threads; my heart is in turmoil, and the clear tea is hard to sip in its stead.
In the river’s heart, the fishing fires seem about to sleep; heavy is the jade hairpin—how can I pillow this spring sorrow deep?

Immortals at the Magpie Bridge

Among the clouds, the stars scatter; in the river’s heart, the moon melts away; how many blossoms has the courtyard lost today?
Down the secluded, deep path I wish to seek; yet I fear there is nowhere for my steps to speak.
New wine in a golden goblet, green dregs floating light; behind the curtain, a faint chill and the rain of night.
Ten thousand sorrowful thoughts are shaken again by the wind; breathing the dragon-brain incense, its fragrance follows where my dreams haveinned.

Immortals at the Magpie Bridge

The swing sways to and fro, early birds sing of spring; dots of delicate blossoms hide where the willows cling.
Outside the city, fragrant grasses are greener than the sky; sweat dampens my華衣 (splendid robes) and blue sleeves high.
A Penglai fairyland, heavenly brocade and kingfisher-green, surpassed not even by distant peaks emerging from the clouds’ sheen.
Several gusts of the long wind indulge their wildness free, only blowing wrinkles across the river’s heart to see.

Immortals at the Magpie Bridge

Gusts of pure breeze, resplendent moonlight’s grace; in the dimness, I pour fine wine alone in this place.
Gazing to the ends of the earth, the road is endless and vast; the house is deep and quiet, my heart in dejection cast.
At the Magpie Bridge they have met, the magpies’ cries have dispersed; though magpie feathers fill the street, who cares for the cursed?
Water is clear, moistening jade—jade both square and round; the night is solitary and cold, my ghostly soul returns to yesterday’s ground.

Sixteen-Character Lyric

Home—
One gaze across the misty streams where evening rains roam.
Brushing past flying geese, the moon’s reflection rocks on the autumn river’s foam.

Untitled

Early birds call out note by note, summoning my dreams back home; o’er green hills, the morning sun sprinkles spring light’s foam.
Thick green leaves conceal the gauzy mist; along the endless ancient steps, crape myrtles twist.
The east wind understands not the blossoms’ heart; with pale hands I lightly pluck them, treading duckweed as I depart.

Remembering the Qin Maiden

The sound of rain falls on and on;
In the small shop across the street, a solitary lamp shines wan.
A solitary lamp shines wan;
With bowed head I wait in vain, while all others have already gone.

The moon rises, the wind sobs, about to set forth into the dark;
In the cold pond, no stars at the sky’s edge leave a mark.
Stars at the sky’s edge leave no mark;
Promised, yet thou comest not—the rain falls with a ceaseless spark.

Joy of Meeting

Carrying spring, a fine rain falls in the courtyard’s space,
Lush and green its grace.
In the emerald trees, how many orioles warble, sharing the spring wind’s embrace?

Spring’s splendor is heavy, spring’s colors tease, and my mood melts away;
Strolling idly down the flower-path beneath the willows’ shade, we meet again today.

Remembering the Qin Maiden

Passing deep into the wood,
Tender buds of fresh green hear a sparse sound where they stood.
Hear a sparse sound where they stood;
Brushing aside light smoke, through bamboo crevices a breeze is brewed.

Year after year, when the snow is spent, new roots spring forth;
In garden after garden, flower stamens renew their fragrant worth.
Renew their fragrant worth;
How much pent-up sorrow is there? Let it all be consigned to the golden goblet’s girth.

Untitled

The moonlight takes up the pen of a shooting star
To write whispers of love to the myriad stars afar.

In the autumn wind of the courtyard,
Fallen leaves recount the tale of parting hard.

Twilight drapes itself in splendid, iridescent clouds;
Whither flies the lost bird through the shrouds?

Night after night, I chant your book of verse,
Fantasizing news of your return to rehearse.

Sands of the Washing Stream

Flying swallows, light smoke, and willows of azure-green;
Behind the clouds in the vast sky, moonlight pours its sheen.
Reed-pipes and flutes are like water, the night like ice keen.

Beating a fan with flowing tassels, the wind turns gentle and mild;
In the courtyard of fallen blossoms, the rain is clear and undefiled.
A jasper cup of emerald wine reflects a sky with stars piled.

Gazing at Jiangnan

O stars of heaven, shining upon my mat’s light chill!
Ten thousand threads of tender grief are too much to bear; a thousand bitter longings climb the balustrade still.
When the lamp dies, it is harder yet to endure the thrill.

Gazing at Jiangnan

Soft, rosy hands tease and stir my heart’s core.
Cold snow beats against the window, keeping me from sleep; a lone star circles the heavenly hook all night o’er.
Tears fall, harder yet to gather than before.

Gazing at Jiangnan

A goblet of crystal glass cannot bear the evening wind’s sway.
Evening rain, clear frost, and the moon at the river’s floor; a skiff leaves the bank in the driving rain’s fray.
Outside the pavilion stands a cold, solitary bridge of gray.

Gazing at Jiangnan

Wild geese on the sandy shoal break through the smoke in the evening light’s glow.
Reeds rustle mournfully as the wind sighs; by the long pavilion, the cold moon lingers slow.
With knitted brows, I recall thy dark tresses of long ago.

Gazing at Jiangnan

After twilight falls, the moon’s shadow grows more desolate still.
Over turbid wine, to whom can I pour out my bitter breast? The clear, cold night enters the casement sill.
All o’er the ground, cold frost piles its chill.

Palindrome Poem

The frigid river mirrors the moon in the cold wind’s swift flight; the quiet courtyard congeals with frost where autumn leaves fade.
Where faded leaves and autumn frost congeal, the courtyard is quiet; swift wind and cold moon mirror the river’s frigid shade.

Untitled

Within the walls of Chang’an, from whose upper chamber flies the music of a jade flute?
Past all the bustling clamor, carefree spring blossoms and emerald willows sway mute.
Migrating wild geese cry with urgency; a letter is hard to entrust, and one weeps alone.
The night is quiet and still; rolling up the blind, the cold wind embraces my traveler’s gown.

Fisherman’s Song

Twirling the ruined splendor of spring within my hand,
Who is it that stands wan and haggard in the east wind’s land?
The bright moon is cold, the rain falls misty and grand;
Dripping upon my heart, my sorrow grows harder to withstand.

Two Modern-Vernacular Regulated Verses

If I should become a little bird, I would seek out the crimson of the flame;
With my heart’s blood I would scorch the icy wilds, then swiftly die amidst the hell of calamity’s frame.

If I should become a green leaf, I would drive away that flying insect pest;
With my broad garments of green, I would shield against the gale in the sky’s crest.

Sands of the Washing Stream

A single tune of Yangguan holds ten thousand threads of grace;
A frosty sky steeps the moon as a shooting star skims space;
Though fleeting light scatters completely, my heart finds no peaceful place.

Night’s hue descends upon me, and in sorrow alone I lean.

The Seventh Night

In the idle courtyard, blossoms thrive by the pond-side willow tree; tonight, the myriad stars are naturally different to see.
The bright moon roams alone within the Silver Sea; twin shining stars meet upon the Magpie Bridge free.
Fluttering flying sleeves are lifted by the pure breeze; trailing rainbow skirts stain tearful cheeks with crimson decrees.
May lovers in the mortal realm endure forevermore; high in the tower we drink together till dawn invades the eastern shore.

Pride of the Fisherman

Boundless the sleet and snow, fierce the wind’s might; the winter plum suffers not from the cold winter’s blight.
Its stamens bloom with secluded fragrance, still charming and bright;
Deep within the woods, where a hundred flowers have perished, one may still reach its height.

The pale moon lingers fondly as frost melts on the ground; in the idle courtyard, swallows call that spring is homeward bound.
Fallen petals of red jade blossoms are like tears profound;
Though its body dies, riding the wind afar, its fragrance is left to the world around.

Untitled

A cold window without a moon.
Dim starlight, and a bitter cicada chirping with urgency.
I cannot bear to draw the pearl curtains close, only fearing that on the morrow, the gentle light will be drowned.
The candle flame has just gone out, and a chill, fierce wind scrapes past my side.
Secret resentment surges, my eyes can scarce endure it—how can I bear these tears pouring forth in a torrent!

Wounded in form, every word is written in fresh blood.
Having lost a dear friend, I know well who is the lesser!
Why do I sigh long without a word? Where there are tears, could it ever be joy?
Through the long, endless night, only the warm candle before me speaks.
The wooden desk is cold, and my heart is equally chill; the brush is withered, and the lamp-oil has just run dry.

To be continued

entry.title: Diary of May 13th
Sunday night
I have lived a happy life.
entry.content:
I Have Lived a Happy Life

Is a psychiatric hospital akin to arresting patients in advance just to prevent crimes? Even if it is so-called voluntary, how can a person possess the freedom to renounce their own freedom.
How can people pay the price for things they have never done?
As for dangerous mentally ill patients, perhaps they can only be judged after they have an episode? A headache of a question.

At my father’s funeral, I did not feel the slightest bit of dejection or sorrow over his death; the only thing that left a deep impression was the physiologically sickening atmosphere of the funeral, the jarring clamor of pipes and strings, the wailing echoing across the wilds.
During the seven years from the first grade of primary school to the first year of junior high, I only met with them during winter and summer vacations. All other times could be completely described as utterly devoid of tidings. Perhaps at some point, he was cast far behind by me into my kindergarten childhood; throughout the entirety of primary school, the only ones close to me were my paternal grandparents.
Even during winter and summer vacations, I began to doubt whether my smiles toward my parents were a seamless disguise,
The difference between a real smile and a fake smile perhaps lies in whether it can be stopped immediately at will. Many of my smiles toward my mother now are obviously active, controlled smiles.
Like Lao Laizi playing the fool to amuse his parents.

There are a few things that exist in my memories: in the lower grades, out of anger, I refused to communicate with my mother over the phone many times, yet when I subsequently received the plastic toy soldiers sent by my mother, the coexistence of guilt and joy seemed to prove that my anger was likewise a disguise. A disguised emotion.
Because I heard my homeroom teacher say that a certain classmate’s parent worked out of town, yet drove hundreds of kilometers to the school just to attend a brief parent-teacher conference… The homeroom teacher’s inexplicable praise made me, at the time, shamelessly make a request to my mother to take a three-hour bus ride to attend the parent-teacher conference; later, my mother didn’t come, and nothing happened either.
I only remember that both sides of the highway were mountain forests shaded in green, just like a map in a racing game. I sat in the car, sometimes spending the entire trip watching three pre-downloaded episodes of iPartment, and sometimes sleeping.

Junior High

In junior high P.E. class, the black-and-white world in my eyes at the time, like Kousei’s, was obviously already different from that of my classmates back then.
“Look at him, so melancholic”
On the sun-drenched cement road, hurrying toward the sports field that was like an execution ground, my classmate’s casual remark echoed endlessly, echoing until now.
Deadpan Bro
A strange title… a strange title… a strange title… a strange title… I seem to have never voiced my opinion to others about my own nickname, even though I indeed felt displeased at times afterward.
But it never reached the point of angry shouting. As long as they are happy, it’s fine, I really mean it.

The medicine ball a classmate accidentally threw toward me did not make me dodge; of course, he missed as well. My heart indeed tangled in complexity for a split second, but ultimately I did not walk away, watching the red medicine ball gradually descend from the backdrop of the blue sky, gradually approaching me, onto the ground two meters away. Perhaps it was a subconscious evasion that kept me from being smashed to death.
“You’re really brave~ Sorry”
He was definitely the most innocent person of our age; he had a bulky build, yet possessed the smile of a child, as if every class would have such a figure. He scratched his head and walked away to my right; my expression didn’t change much, all blankness and sorrow, and the clouds of blankness and sorrow have shrouded me to this day.

In order to cater to possible customs, in order to make myself look more approachable, perhaps to curry favor with or reassure my classmates, on the first day of boarding at school, in the narrow dormitory aisle, on my lower bunk bed, I stripped stark naked, and tremblingly took my shampoo and body wash to the shower room. Even though at home I was only required by my grandfather to take a bath once a week, and wash my hair once, at school I was so bold.
Heh
I want to tear this memory to shreds.

ZYX

My primary school crush is not in the same class as me!!! Alas!!!
I’m going to die,
…
I still like her. She is so cute, after entering high school, she seems to still be as cute as she was in primary school, so cute,

I really like her expression; it is not a smile with a dagger hidden behind it, it is sincere alertness, it is an expression that could not be more real, it is the same expression, as mine.
I still remember in primary school when she wore fluffy, cute clothes, sat down next to my seat, and started acting out English words. I clearly remember there were two fluffy little pom-poms on her clothes, extremely cute.
She is extremely cute.
I miss her so much.
But I simply cannot talk to anyone at all.
I simply cannot talk to anyone at all, therefore I simply cannot have any communication with her, I seem to have lost the ability to converse.
But, really, just by seeing her, I am so happy.

June 5, 2021, sadly took two weeks of leave at home, the college entrance exam is next week, forced to continue taking leave.
Every time, I schedule my suicide for right when I return to school.

However, even if by the railing I have imagined ten thousand times myself climbing onto the railing like a gymnast, leaning my body outward, and then plummeting into a pool of blood,
if it has never once been put into practice, how can one say that the probability of him committing suicide is high?

Aren’t we all thinking about suicide at every single moment?

entry.title: The Colors of Youth
entry.content:
The Colors of Youth

Like the colorful ribbon in the distant sky just as the rain clears, the newborn sunlight radiates with color. In youth, at the starting point of life, who dyes us in different colors? Ourselves.

Youth is crimson, like the morning sun emerging from a sky just torn from black chaos—unbridled passion scattering boundless golden light across the vast world. We still hold vivid dreams, we still have poetry and distant horizons, and we still possess the wild arrogance to change everything.

With spirits high and lofty thoughts in flight, we fain would scale the azure skies to clasp the moon so bright.

Burying ourselves deep within mountains of books, roaming through oceans of test papers.

A time shall come to cleave the waves upon the gale, and o’er the vasty deep to hoist my cloudy sail.

Though monstrous waves may surge to the skies, the little boat carrying dreams and hopes shall not perish; a sky filled with gray clouds and ink-black rain cannot blind our burning crimson eyes, believing that miracles will surely emerge from afar once more.
The crimson, warm flame within our hearts makes us fearless against the freezing ice and flying snow at five in the morning; we leap from our beds and covers, thus beginning a day of study.
The sound of reading in the classroom awakens the world before the lazy sun; amidst pitch darkness, it is as if we carry the light. Running on the sports field, we do not fear the sweat and dirt covering our cheeks; strings of flying beads of sweat are the symbol of vitality.

Youth is also a warm tangerine.
Along the endless night road, an old, yellowish lamp keeps watch by the wayside, as if it has waited alone in the night for so long just for your arrival. This is that warm friendship. When a frail body trembles in the biting wind, when powerless hands grow numb in the ice and snow, when a hollow gaze blurs in the white storm, friendship is that warm tangerine lamp waiting for you in the distance, standing steady and unmoving amidst the flying snow. The lamp draws closer, closer, and ever closer; treading upon the pure white snow, she comes to your side. The pale rain and snow melt into the warm lamplight and the warm heart. Embracing friendship, our hearts are refueled and regain their warmth, and the blooming flowers of our hearts can once again blossom proudly amidst a sky full of wind and snow. And all of this is given to us by the tangerine, warm friendship beside us. We embrace our friendship so passionately that the world becomes nothing more than her soft, gentle body.

Youth is a tranquil deep blue.
Marveling at the rich knowledge of mathematics, physics, and chemistry in our minds, intoxicated by the cultivation of a soul well-versed in poetry, and finding peace in the nourishing rain and dew of books from ancient to modern times, both Chinese and foreign. We begin to sketch our initial views of the world in our hearts, begin to establish the yardsticks of value, and begin to look toward and plan the possible lives of our future. With blue tranquility, we confront dark terrors. Our confidence is a deep blue composure amidst crimson passion.

However, youth also holds that lost, depressed foggy gray, and pitch black.
Alone in the pitch-black dead of night, inside cold, stiff covers, tasting the teardrops that slide down one by one; a sensitive soul feeling deep, throbbing pain from an unintentional word or action of others; a momentary stern glance from teachers or parents shakes us to the core, filling us with endless terror, causing tears to burst their banks in an instant; in our anxiety, we peer through the brick walls of the dormitory, counting imaginary stars and sheep—given wings, they can roam freely in the sea of stars, while before our eyes there is only a dilapidated gray brick wall, and outside the window, only a lone tree standing stiff and dead like a night watchman; troubled in mind and spirit, we might skip a meal, skip a day of food, skip three days of food, until we faint at some point and the fact of our fasting is finally discovered; we sit in the gloomy classroom, driven by pent-up melancholy, using a pen to pierce through book pages, listening with morbid joy to the sound of tearing; we might suddenly pick up a pocketknife, and amidst a few stunned gazes, carve chaotic patterns into our arms—perhaps it is beautiful, who knows, why is something only beautiful if they say it is?—and then quietly watch the fresh blood flow, and flow, across the textbook; we might fly into a rage, and in our anger destroy the most beloved doll we have cherished for years, or kick away the poor little kitten that accompanied us for years, which we once held in our arms and rubbed against our cheeks affectionately, staring blankly at their corpses; we fear socializing, fear the flowing crowds, fear standing up in class, fear answering questions, fear standing at the back of the classroom, fear the teacher standing beside us, fear the teacher bending down to look at what I am writing…; we might still be afraid of the dark just like when we were children, planting countless grotesque monsters from our imagination around the unlit night road, all plotting how to harm me; and eventually, we will come to fear the height of buildings, and whether climbing over the railing or not, we gaze for a long, long time at the concrete bricks below, checking if anyone is passing by around us. Could the bright colors of youth really outnumber the dark ones?

Youth is vibrant and colorful, and we endow it with the colors we like. Yet sometimes the paintbrush is in our own hands, and sometimes it is snatched away, stolen, and snapped in two by others. The dark colors upon us can thus only come from the smearing of others.

This was an exam essay from last year. In order to get through the exam, the original text was much more positive and upbeat than this, though the overall outline remains unchanged; I merely modified much of the phrasing. As a result, it has become slightly longer than the original.

entry.title: Three Short Stories
entry.content:
Vignette One

She stood alone on the edge of the rooftop.
With her glasses taken off,
the lights blurred her distant vision.
The lights hid before her, behind square panes of glass and blue clay bricks.
A bat suddenly darted past, startling the rustling rats.

The night wind lifted the hem of her skirt, swept her body down, closed her eyes,
and blew this world away.

Vignette Two

She was the finest child in the entire academy; she was nothing short of light itself.
On any occasion, she was always the most eye-catching.
Her seat was in the corner by the window, where sunlight never ceased to spill upon her desk,
and outside the window, the white birds of summer never ceased to fly past, time and again, humming songs of every hue.

Back then, with a faint smile, she narrowed her right eye at the gazes of her teacher and classmates, drew a circle in the air with her left hand,
and leaped smilingly from the fourth floor;
even that thunderous crash failed to awaken those vacant stares.

Vignette Three

The night had grown deep.
She looked to the left of the desk, where the only light was flickering.
Laid out on the desk were twelve pills of quetiapine, two bottles of two hundred chlorpheniramine pills, twenty pills of sertraline, ten pills of lorazepam,
one hundred milliliters of benzene, and one hundred milliliters of ethylene glycol.

She wanted to go to a place with no people,
a place where there would never, ever, ever be any people.
She was so afraid of people; she wanted to go to a place devoid of humankind.
She stared fixedly at the hideous face in the shattered mirror, and the one accusing her said: “Go die.”

Written on 2020.10.13, during evening self-study

entry.title: Analysis of myself
entry.content:
The conclusion I have vaguely come to is that my thoughts are too complex.
I once viewed all of my actions as a negation of others, to the extent that existence itself was seen as a sin. It was in this frame of mind that Yozo prayed and left Junko. Yet in school, what right do I have to leave? Because I view leaving school as a sin, too—a negation of others. —An internal monologue:

“You are all so kind, treating me so very well. Then why am I still like this? It can only be my own fault. Not a single person has insulted me, bullied me, or mocked me—all of the above, whether viewed objectively or subjectively by me, are things you have never done. Yet the fact that I am in pain, I am certain beyond a doubt. Then the only remaining possible option is myself. The cause of everything is my own mental self-harm. Can I only waste your care, having never once given any good response? Even though things are getting better—my bad influence on you is shrinking step by step. At least in my actions, I am becoming more and more transparent. Yet I am still terrified of polluting your sight. Thus, inaction also contains the action of “existing.” Once again, through the action of “existence,” I am negating you.

The world is a stage of affirmation. While I hide far away in a corner, not daring to breathe, terrified of any element of negation in my actions, and thus abandoning action altogether. My pain stems from a dissatisfaction with negation—existence, and self-affirmation. The failure to negate the negation; negation is negating everything except itself.

The only thing that affected me deeply, that was PTSD-like, was in the summer of 2018, that vast black space emerging in my mind. That person kneeling down.

The frequent longing for death that emerged in my first year of middle school, and the sudden, overwhelming change of environment in my first year of high school, made the nightmare surface completely. The years spent as a left-behind child after parting from my mother in first grade are probably the wellspring of my introversion.

When I have no affirmation for myself in my heart, please do not encourage me. I will think you are hypocritical, that you are deceiving me, and the backlash will be even more severe.

When no one is around, I feel fine.

I have never blamed you.

I love spatial solitude, I love it so much.

Note

Originally, I intended to write this to the grade director, because school had just started back then and I was very unaccustomed to it. He gave me a lot of help. So I wrote a letter to introduce myself to him. For me, written words are much simpler than spoken words, much more comfortable. Many of the views above I no longer agree with now.

entry.title: How to explain Yozo using Schopenhauer's theory
entry.content:
A person who has only ever negated himself fears others’ affirmation of his own will.
Because, faintly seeing through the principle of individuation, he realizes that this affirmation of himself is so intense. Even though this affirmation is not made by himself, this affirmation still increases the absolute value of the affirmation of the will; through and according to the principle of individuation, this is also a negation of the other, and at the same time, his own negation of the other.
This is his own negation of others—one directed at the other, which he had never dared to make before, yet has now been automatically made by the other.
Yozo’s sensitivity views this as a crime akin to murder.
Thus Yozo kneels behind the door, praying that the lover killed by him might be freed from the pain of his own fantasies. In order to avoid committing an even greater crime————negation, he flees.

Yozo faintly sees through the principle of individuation, and thus is called “a child like God.”
Even though all of them do not realize this.

Presumed written in 2020.9

entry.title: Golden Ocean
entry.content:
The setting sun generously scattered its golden light upon every living consciousness in the world. He stood alone at the edge of the cliff, the sea breeze lifting the hem of his clothes, the azure silk lingering like waves. He slowly raised his left hand before him and uncurled his five fingers, revealing a single teardrop—a crystal like a teardrop—countless tiny edges and facets clustered together, glinting with the afterglow floating far upon the sea’s horizon, melting that scorching yet icy flame into an icy yet scorching teardrop. With brows slightly furrowed, he gazed dazedly at her tear. Unknowingly, his own tears blurred the entire world.

The year she turned 16, a grand coming-of-age ceremony prompted the villagers to build a bridge for all the 16-year-old children, a colossal bridge, a great bridge connecting the sea cliff to the evening glow. No one could remember, when the bridge was finally completed, how many citizens from city-states came to offer congratulations, how many noble kings came to pay homage, how many majestic popes came to bestow their blessings. Yet now, no one was old enough to remember how the villagers accomplished this feat; they could only remember when the 16-year-old maidens, wearing gorgeous dresses, adorned with bracelets inlaid with 101 pearls harvested from clam shells at the bottom of the deep sea—the villagers’ accumulation over past decades—and wearing silk hats with white feathers slanted in them, walked barefoot onto the bridge, walking further and further away… further and further away… until finally, only she returned, carrying the evening glow in a bottle, while the other girls vanished forever into that eternal evening glow.
She soon faced deliberate hostility from the villagers; she was deemed a murderous executioner, deemed a selfish wretch worthy of everyone’s spittle, deemed an inhumane traitor. People could freely spit filthy saliva onto her pure white cheeks without worrying about any possible reprimand, and she was used by the boys as a tool to vent their lust; whenever night fell, animals would gather in the jungle, nibbling away at her heart. She tried to resist, but it only invited more painful experiences
Finally, that dreadful day arrived along with an all-night torrential rain that crushed the door; before the morning glow even appeared, her mother was taken away by a dozen of the most brutal burly men organized by the village. Her mother struggled, refusing to leave, forcibly tearing apart the hard threshold with her fragile fingernails, leaving ten distinct and horrifying trails of blood, stretching from the attic to the doorway, stretching from the gravel-paved cobblestone path to the green field dotted with colorful little flowers, from the cement ground all the way to that most unknowable, secret place—forced into prostitution—for even though she had lost her ten fingers, she still possessed a mouth and genitals… Her father was killed in his sleep—brutal bandits hacked off his head with a blunt axe—her father’s blood-dripping head was hung in front of her house, and that face, which had once given her countless laughs, still held a smile melted into his dreams… The remainder of her father’s body was stolen from the funeral home in plain sight of all, and no one would step forward to stop that sinful corpse. The chance for a cremation, which she had traded her body countless times to obtain, vanished.
Her father’s grave was empty, just like the tiny chambers of her heart.
“I’ll probably die soon too…”, dressed in rags, she knelt blankly before the grave, her disheveled long hair and crimson pupils making anyone who saw her at first glance feel an urge to protect her—yet her desolate, cold gaze radiated infinite terror. The surrounding ocean of green was so deep, as if it too were plotting to kill her.
“What should I do? Father? Father…” With fists stained with dirt and blood, she pounded desperately against the stone tablet again and again. Hollow echoes…
A brown ant climbed up the stone tablet, chasing the golden setting sun. She abruptly stood up and turned around—infinite golden light invaded her eyes, then gradually shrank into a yellow orb. The surrounding purplish-red evening glow was ethereal and unfathomable.
“I should go back…”, murmuring strange words, she walked dazedly toward the west—as if she had already lost her soul, tripped by creeping vines, she stood up and kept moving forward… swallowed by river waters, she stood up and kept moving forward… blocked by high mountains, she went around them and kept moving forward…
“I cannot lose my sun…”
The eternal bridge existed quietly there, connecting the sea cliff with the magnificent evening glow in the distance. He gazed at her retreating figure, silently, silently.
The ocean waves ceased their gasping.
